3.	Since the inception of the radioactive fall-out study program in 1955, the Department of National Health and Welfare has steadily expanded the program by enlarging the area of coverage and including additional samples and analyses as staff, equipment and need developed.
From an initial small network of milk sampling points, the program has expanded until it now includes measurements of fallout in daily air filter samples and monthly precipitation samples from 24 meteorological observing stations, measurement of strontium 90 in annual soil samples from 23 sites and in annual wheat samples from the nine principal wheat growing areas of Canada, measurement of strontium 89, strontium 90, cesium 137 and iodine 131 in fluid milk samples collected 3 times a week from 16 cities across Canada, and measurement of strontium 90 in human bone samples provided by pathologists from various hospitals in Canada.
In addition special equipment for measuring cesium 137 directly in humans is undergoing initial testing. A new departmental laboratory is under construction in Ottawa and the establishment of the radiation protection division is being increased to meet the demands of this comprehensive program. Estimates for the current year provide for new equipment which will be used in these studies.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Labour
maintopic: 'UNEMPLOYMENT INSURANCE CLAIMS, MONTREAL AND QUEBEC CITY
speechtext:
1. All non-contentious claims originating in Quebec city are adjudicated at that point. Contentious claims are sent for adjudication to the regional office in Montreal. Several reasons dictated this procedure, the most important of which were:
(1)	The constant training of qualified staff, to maintain a high standard of adjudication, is not practical when the adjudication staff is dispersed into small units.
(2)	Full utilization of expert adjudication staff is obtainable only where the volume of irregular claims warrants the establishment of such a staff.
(3)	Recruitment of staff with the necessary technical knowledge essential for this function was difficult at many points, and not obtainable at all at other points.
(4)	Consultation with officers having wide knowledge and experience with respect to the adjudication of contentious claims was not possible where only small units were constituted.
(5)	Uniformity of decisions in contentious claims is essential and is attainable only when the claims are dealt with at one point.
2.	None. Over 90 per cent of all claims sent by Quebec city to Montreal are back in Quebec city within three or four days of despatch by the latter. Delays of three to four weeks occur in less than 3 per cent of the claims during the period of heaviest claim load, and, because these delays are necessitated by the need for extended investigation, they would occur If adjudication were to take place in Quebec city.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext:
1. Yes, the department has a comprehensive program designed to determine the levels of radioactive fall-out in Canada as a result of nuclear testing.
The program involves: air sampling (24 stations, daily collection and analysis); precipitation sampling (24 stations, monthly collection and analysis); soil sampling (23 stations, annual collection and analysis); milk sampling (major dairies in 16 cities, three times a week collection, weekly analyses for iodine 131 and monthly analyses for strontium 90 and cesium 137); wheat sampling (nine major wheat producing areas, annual crop samples and analysis); and human bone sampling (collected from hospitals across Canada, as available).
2.	The department is engaged in studies which will make it possible to make better estimates of the radiation dose resulting from radioactive fall-out.
3.	The department has for many years used the recommendations of the international commission on radiological protection as the basis for evaluating radiation levels. Recommendations of other recognized authoritative bodies such as the United States federal radiation council are used when applicable. Members

of the department are also in close touch with recognized scientists in this field in this and other countries.

What flag, or flags, were flown by the armed forces of Canada in world war I and world war II, and upon what authority?

During world wars I and II, the ships of the R.C.N. wore the white ensign and the Canadian blue ensign under authority of order in council P.C. 2843 dated 16 December 1911, the adoption of these ensigns having been ratified at the imperial conference in 1911.
During world war I, the Canadian army flew the union jack.
The red ensign, bearing the 1921 approved shield of the arms of Canada, was subsequently approved by P.C. 134 in 1924 for display outside of Canada on Canadian government property.
During world war II, the following flags were flown by the Canadian army:
(a)	The union flag (jack) which was the flag officially prescribed in King's Regulations and orders, 1939, for the Canadian army until superseded by the Canadian red ensign;
(b)	The Canadian red ensign was authorized by Canadian army routine order 4021 dated 22 January 1944 to be flown at all units of the Canadian army serving with the forces of other nations.
(c)	The Canadian red ensign was authorized by Canadian army overseas routine order 4582 dated 10 May 1944, to be flown overseas on all appropriate occasions by formations and units when serving in the same command, formation or area with or in proximity to British, dominion or allied forces;
(d)	A distinctive Canadian army battle flag was authorized by the cabinet and militia
Questions
council on 7 December 1939, for the commander of the senior Canadian formation overseas and was assigned to the commander first Canadian infantry division when proceeding overseas. This flag is known to have been used on one or two occasions in 1940 in Britain. The flag was a white ensign with the union flag in the upper corner next to the mast; in the centre of the flag, a large sprig of three red maple leaves and in the upper corner at the fly end were three golden fleur-de-lis on a blue roundel.
The R.C.A.F. was not in existence in world war I. In 1923 the Canadian air force was authorized to fly the ensign adopted by the R.A.F. This assent was contained in dispatch 578 of 22 October 1923 from the secretary of state for the colonies to the Governor General.
On 5 July 1940 royal assent was given to alter slightly the design of the ensign as flown by the R.C.A.F. by substituting a small red maple leaf for the red centre roundel. This ensign was flown by the R.C.A.F. in world war II.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
speechtext:
1. The government is concerned about the low supply situation in the Great lakes-Ottawa river drainage and the consequent low water levels in the great lakes and lake St. Louis, and officials are accordingly in daily touch with the situation.

subtopic: ANNOUNCEMENT OF DEATH AND STATEMENT BY PRIME MINISTER

speechtext: On the orders of the day:

speakeroldname: Right Hon. L. B. Pearson (Prime Minister):
subtopic: ANNOUNCEMENT OF DEATH AND STATEMENT BY PRIME MINISTER
speechtext:
If, by unanimous consent, we might revert to motions I should like to make an announcement which has just been brought to my attention, a very sad announcement to the effect that His Holiness the Pope passed away shortly before the house convened this afternoon.
On behalf of the government I have sent a message of sympathy to the apostolic delegate and have also issued the following statement which perhaps I may be permitted to read to the house. The statement is as follows:
May I on behalf of the government and people of Canada express my deep and profound sympathy on the death of His Holiness, Pope John XXIII.
During the relatively short period of his pontificate His Holiness won the admiration and deep respect of peoples of all religious faiths. His dedicated service to the cause of Christian unity, to the freedom and welfare of mankind and, above all, to the realization of the ideals of peace, which only recently he expressed so movingly and impressively, set an example for all men.
His loss will be deeply felt in Canada, as it will throughout the world, but we are the richer for the inspiration of his life, his words and his work.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. J. G. Diefenbaker (Leader of the Opposition):
subtopic: ANNOUNCEMENT OF DEATH AND STATEMENT BY PRIME MINISTER
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I join with the Prime Minister in the words of sympathy he has expressed. My wife and I had a memorable experience within one week after

His Holiness became spiritual head of his church, in that we were received in private audience. I shall always recall that as one of the most impressive privileges which has been mine. In that short half hour he revealed himself as a devout, kindly and, above all, a humble person.
His devotion to the cause of world peace, has, as the Prime Minister said, made him in a few years one of the most renowned popes in modern history, a world voice for peace and the social betterment of all mankind. All of us, without regard to our religious persuasion, recognize him as a leader in Christendom.

subtopic: ANNOUNCEMENT OF DEATH AND STATEMENT BY PRIME MINISTER
speechtext:
On behalf of our group in this house I join with other hon. members in expressing our sympathy and our support of the message which the Prime Minister has so promptly forwarded on this sad occasion.
In the short four and a half years during which Pope John XXIII was head of his church he made a great contribution to the cause of peace, and convinced men of all faiths around the world of his dedication to the causes he stood for and represented so faithfully, and without equivocation, day after day. Thus we join not only with the hon. members of this house but with peace loving, Christian people and men of all faiths around the world who at this time mourn his passing.

subtopic: ANNOUNCEMENT OF DEATH AND STATEMENT BY PRIME MINISTER
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, we in the New Democratic party would like to associate ourselves with the expression of sympathy which has been placed before the house by the Prime Minister at the passing of His Holiness Pope John XXIII. It is undoubtedly true that history will place the late Pope among the great Christian leaders of our time. His two encyclicals, Mater et Magistra and Pacem in Terris, are mountain peaks in Christian expressions of the desire for social justice and peace in our time. Very few Christian leaders have reached out as he has to embrace all mankind and all men of good will, and I think when the story of his life is written it will be summed up in the simple words "Blessed are the peacemakers, for they shall be called the sons of God".

subtopic: RUSSIAN PROPOSAL THAT MEDITERRANEAN BE MADE NUCLEAR-FREE ZONE

speechtext: On the orders of the day:

subtopic: RUSSIAN PROPOSAL THAT MEDITERRANEAN BE MADE NUCLEAR-FREE ZONE
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, may I direct a question to the Prime Minister. In view of a report in the Montreal Gazette of June 1 that "the United States told the disarmament conference the Soviet demand for a nuclear-free zone in the Mediterranean is nonsensical propaganda", does the Prime Minister still hold the view he expressed on May 22 that the Soviet proposal "is a very important proposal indeed"?

speakeroldname: Right Hon. L. B. Pearson (Prime Minister):
subtopic: RUSSIAN PROPOSAL THAT MEDITERRANEAN BE MADE NUCLEAR-FREE ZONE
speechtext:
Yes, Mr. Speaker. I think any proposal coming from the Soviet Union is likely to be an important proposal, and I think this was an important proposal. As my hon. friend gave me notice that he was going to raise this question, perhaps I might say a word about it. Indeed, I indicated that I would when it came up previously.
Although it is not possible to state one over-all policy with respect to the question of denuclearised zones, it should be recognized that any such proposal must meet at least three criteria. First, it should be acceptable to the countries of the geographical area in which the zone would be located. That seems to be obvious. Second, it should
Inquiries of the Ministry include some arrangement for verifying that the commitments undertaken would be carried out. And third, it should be consistent with the accepted principle that no disarmament measure should create a unilateral advantage for any state or group of states.
As to the first point, Mr. Speaker, the Soviet proposal does not involve Canada directly, though it certainly involves Canada as would any proposal which might have some bearing on the easing of tensions. Therefore, while it does not involve Canada directly we shall have to await the considered reaction of the countries to which it was addressed before we come to a considered conclusion ourselves. The reports we have had so far indicate that it does not have the support of all the countries concerned.
With regard to the second and third criteria, there is no mention of procedures for verifying that obligations undertaken would be carried out; and there has apparently been no attempt to maintain equality and balance among the states concerned. This situation, of course, might be altered in the course of negotiations if negotiations began. I mentioned, for example, in my original reply to the hon. member that it would be interesting to know whether the Mediterranean zone would include the Black sea; the text of the proposal suggests that it does not, and that in fact it involves no territory in which the Soviet Union is directly involved. As such, its effect would be to achieve a unilateral advantage for the Soviet Union, a result which would not be likely to contribute to the relaxation of tension.
Nevertheless, Mr. Speaker, despite these obvious shortcomings and the propagandistic tone and timing of the proposal, I want to assure the house that its exact terms are being given and will be given careful study, as will the reactions of the countries most directly concerned, and that any possibilities it may hold out for constructive steps to reduce the danger of war will certainly be taken into account in determining our final position on this matter.

When we adjourned on Friday, I had the floor. I understand the Minister of Justice wishes to make a statement. I shall be glad to give way to him but I should like the privilege of speaking in the debate later, after he has concluded his remarks, if I may.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I am grateful to the hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam for allowing me to deal with the matters with which I should like to deal at the
moment. They have to do with certain questions that were raised by hon. members of the New Democratic party on Friday when, unfortunately, I could not be present in the house to hear what they had to say. I was attending a meeting of a subcommittee of cabinet and, for that reason, was unavoidably absent.
I can tell the house, and hon. members who have taken part in this debate that, while I was not here, certain of my colleagues brought to my attention the remarks that were made by these members, and I have also had an opportunity of reading Hansard very carefully. I need hardly say that I am concerned about some of the statements that were made, and I should like to deal with them in such a manner as will enable the house and members, I am sure, to realize that I have taken great care in what I am about to say. I should like, if I may, to divide my remarks into two parts. I should like to put on Hansard, first of all, the policy as I see it that has been declared in the house over the years by previous ministers and by a previous prime minister and then, if I may, I should like to deal in as detailed a manner as I can with the complaints that were made in this house.
I think one has to go, sir, to 1946 to find, not the first pronouncement but one of importance, and that is why I begin in that year. Ever since 1946, when the royal commission on espionage stressed the part played by Canadian communists in the Soviet espionage network exposed by Igor Gouzenko, the Canadian government has shown itself to be acutely aware of the communist threat to the internal security of Canada, particularly that posed by espionage.
On December 3, 1951, the then prime minister, Mr. St. Laurent, speaking to the house on the subject of personnel security in defence industry in general and of the undesirability of holding security appeal hearings in particular, declared, with tacit reference to the Russian intelligence service:
This organization acts with a ruthlessness, and a readiness to sacrifice its own followers, which we find it almost impossible to appreciate. It is only by careful, long continued and patient work that means have been established by our police forces of getting information about the operations of this organization. The organization would be more than ready to precipitate hearings involving their own followers, even if it meant the personal ruin of those individuals, if the hearings would lay bare the sources of information that the police have established.
The same awareness of the espionage threat and of the need for secrecy with respect to counter-espionage is apparent from statements made to this house on June 3, 1954

by the then minister of justice, Mr. Garson, who stated as follows:
We are all aware that the practice of espionage and counter-espionage, the contest between enemy nations to secure and to prevent the securing of intelligence involves the building up, as completely as possible, of a large mass of information; and oftentimes the answer in the affirmative or negative to some simple statement of fact may be the last item needed to complete the general pattern of, if I may use that figure of speech, the jig-saw puzzle which the intelligence department is trying to put together; and this last simple answer may finally determine what that whole pattern is.
Then there is this significant paragraph:
In counter-espionage work there is therefore only one safe policy to follow, and that is the policy of complete reticence about our counter-espionage and complete reticence in respect of the espionage against which we are trying to protect Canada.
The result of these two statements is in effect to say this, that it is very necessary for all our counter-intelligence activities that they be not publicized and they have to be secret in order to be effective. Then it was stated some time later that when a government department seeks information of a sensitive nature it calls upon the Royal Canadian Mounted Police to make an investigation or to make a report, and that investigation and that report is a factual one, and a factual one only. It is then up to the department concerned, either the head or the deputy head of the department, to determine what use he shall make of that information. I make that point, Mr. Chairman, because it has been the policy so far, as I understand it at least, that it is the department concerned that makes the decision upon the report that is received from the R.C.M.P.
In the earliest statements on this subject it was made clear to the house that the Royal Canadian Mounted Police had a fact finding role only and, indeed, that it was very reluctant even to go about securing the information, agreeing to do so only on the understanding that the government department submitting the request for screening would be responsible for determining whether the civil servant in question was to be entrusted with classified information. This, it appears to me, continued to be the policy until 1957 when the then minister of justice, Mr. Fulton, stated in the house the following:
We have absolutely no information to Indicate that we would be justified in relaxing the security precautions that we took with regard to subversive activities in this country.
He made known to the house at that time the following new information concerning the force's role in security screening, namely the requirements to make "an evaluation, if asked, as to the nature of any subversive organization to which the person concerned
Interim Supply
may be shown to have belonged" and to assess "the reliability of information". This was based on the fact that we all know that those who serve the state must be loyal. The loyalty of the civil servant is expected by the government. It is a condition precedent to his employment, and the responsibility for his loyalty rests upon the head of each department or agency.
Coming to investigations on university campuses, Mr. Chairman, these were first raised in 1961 and since, and the R.C.M.P. and the government was asked to cease these attempts to interfere in and, indeed, smear the student body. On that subject, on May 24, 1961 the then minister of justice, Mr. Fulton, had this to say:
Enquiries by the R.C.M.P. into all matters, including security, are carried out in privacy and information regarding them is never given except to persons properly entitled thereto. Any knowledge that such enquiries are being made, or any comments reaching the press, must therefore, on such occasions come from those involved in or contacted during the course of such enquiries. This, of course, completely refutes any suggestions of smear on the part of the R.C.M.P.
There are other statements which were made by the then minister of justice, Mr. Fulton, and I would just like to put one other on Hansard which I am sure has already been brought to the notice of hon. members:
I have never heard it said that it was an infraction of a person's rights if he was asked a question. This is a new concept to me. I endeavoured to indicate in the brief statement I made on opening the R.C.M.P. estimates that we do have a communist threat in Canada. I am not stating anything new when I say that. It is our responsibility, then, to keep a constant check on the size, extent and efficiency of the progress being made by the communists.
I have no doubt that there is concern, grave concern, not only on the part of hon. members in this house but also on the part of the security and intelligence branch of the R.C.M.P. about activities on university campuses. It is an avowed objective of the communists of Canada to infiltrate universities; to infiltrate a number of other organizations whose purposes, though proper, they could subvert to their own ends. As my predecessors in office have stated, I can say that I do not wish university campuses to be unduly subjected to security investigations. Nevertheless, I do not think it would be the right thing to grant them special exemption in this regard, because of what I have thus far stated.
If an investigation into subversion or espionage leads to a university campus, I do not think any hon. member in this house would suggest that the government should terminate the investigation at the boundaries of the campus. If this view is held, then any

Interim, Supply
other organization or association would have an equal right to expect similar treatment on this basis, and then the internal security of the country would become ludicrous.
I come now to the second part of my remarks and I would like to deal with the complaints and statements that were put on Hansard by hon. gentlemen last Friday. The hon. member for Winnipeg North raised the question concerning the surveillance of certain groups of people. Let me say to him that the R.C.M.P. are not interested in the organizations to which the hon. member seems to refer. However, as I stated earlier, the R.C.M.P. is interested in communist activity and when such organizations are penetrated the activities of the communists in them become of interest to the R.C.M.P. The hon. member may be interested in knowing that not infrequently officials of such organizations come to the R.C.M.P. for advice on the problems arising from communist penetration of their groups. Indeed-and I say this in all fairness-the group to which the hon. member belongs has had some experience in these matters, if I am to believe newspaper reports covering the expulsion of persons belonging to the "young socialist alliance" which, according to the press, is "a Trotskyist organization ... a heretic branch of the communist movement". A further point to which the hon. member for Winnipeg North referred is the matter of complaints and criticism in leading Canadian newspapers. That is true. On the other hand there are laudatory statements in newspapers about the work of the R.C.M.P. and if he were to weigh one against the other, I think the hon. member would come to the conclusion that there are far more in the latter class than in the former.
With reference to the question arising out of representations which have been made by the Canadian association of university teachers, I have received from that association a letter which I propose to answer, and I think the committee would agree with me that it would be improper for me to say anything on this subject at this time when I have not yet prepared a reply to this letter.
Is that department as slow as it used to be?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
No. The letter was brought to my attention over the week end and it was difficult, because of what I am doing now, to prepare the kind of reply which I think is necessary in this case. I propose at this time in view of all that has been said about security inquiries on university campuses to point out to this committee that it is not unknown for university authorities to appeal to the R.C.M.P. for advice on problems arising from communist activities on their respective

campuses. Many members of faculties in several universities have voiced fear of communist activities in universities. Indeed, police interest in communist activities in universities is often sparked by information gratuitously received.
I should like to correct an impression which has been made by the hon. member for Winnipeg North, that Commissioner Harvison's interview with the Canadian University Press was published only in Alberta. This interview was carried in nearly every university paper in Canada, and therefore no finger was being pointed at the University of Alberta.
The hon. member also refers to the use of the word "evaluated" by the commissioner in his reference to reports supplied to other government departments. Information is received by the force from many sources. In sending reports to departments it has been found prudent after many years of experience to evaluate the reliability of the sources as "usually reliable" or "of known" or as of "unknown reliability". This has been found necessary in order that the department concerned may properly assess the information the force supplies. May I point out that Commissioner Harvison and his predecessors have consistently objected to any attempt to have the force make decisions on behalf of departmental security authorities? I would like to make it clear that the R.C.M.P. does not make any decision for a department on whether or not an employee is suited for any particular responsibility. The hon. member was quite inaccurate, therefore, when he referred to a "kangaroo court" in the matter of R.C.M.P. handling of these matters.
In quoting from the University Press article the hon. member refers to NATO. The commissioner did not state, or even suggest, that Canada held all the military secrets of NATO. He did say, and quite rightly, that Canada holds some NATO secrets which it is the duty of Canada to protect properly.

On a question of privilege. The minister is questioning a statement I made. I read the commissioner's statement into the record. The record did not say "all," but neither did it say "some". I think the minister should stick to the facts.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I do not think that is a question of privilege. It may well be a question of rebuttal in answer to what I am putting on record, if he feels I have put his position inaccurately. But I certainly did not intend to do that. I think, perhaps, the hon. member should have the right to reply.
May I go a step further and say that the commissioner's reply to Maclean's magazine was made with the authority of my predecessor, the former minister of justice. It

was made by special delivery to the editor of the magazine and Mr. Katz, on a Saturday morning and it was not released to the press until the following Monday. I might add that Mr. Katz' article was published without the commissioner being given an opportunity to comment on its contents, although I understand this was to have beeen done. Furthermore, the editor of Maclean's saw fit to make a reply to the commissioner's letter although he did not see fit to publish it. The commissioner did not, as the hon. member for Winnipeg North suggests, ignore nearly all the charges in the article-he referred specifically to a number of them. As for the case with regard to Huntington college, Sudbury, to which the article referred, I should like to put on record in Hansard the reply which was made to that letter by the former minister of justice, Mr. Fleming. I think it is useful that this should be put on record. The letter reads as follows:
The Reverend Edward T. Lute, B.A., B.D., M.A., Registrar and Associate Professor of Philosophy, Huntington College,
83 Larch Street Sudbury, Ontario.
Dear Sir:
I am replying to the letter of yourself and your colleagues, dated February 28, 1963, concerning the discussions of constable Wiebe, of the Royal Canadian Mounted Police, with the Reverend Dr. J. W. E. Newbery. Inquiries have been made at the Sudbury detachment of the Royal Canadian Mounted Police, on the instructions of the commissioner, to ascertain the facts.
I am advised that constable Wiebe called on the Reverend Dr. Newbery concerning three young men who, according to newspaper reports, were marching from the west coast to Berlin in some form of peace march. Newspaper reports indicated that this group formed the Vancouver-to-Berlin peace campaigners. Whether East or West Berlin was not specified.
According to local press reports Dr. Newbery had arranged for a press conference with these young men and, apparently, had some knowledge of them and, as one of them was reported to be a German national and a former cadet officer in the Hitler youth movement. Constable Wiebe approached Dr. Newbery, who at no time made any objection whatsoever to discussing the matter nor in any way indicated that he was displeased at being approached.
I am also advised that constable Wiebe deliberately endeavoured to make it clear to Dr. Newbery that he was in no way investigating any member of the faculty, or any member of the student body at Huntington college or Laurentian University. Constable Wiebe states that he made this point when he first met Dr. Newbery and, again, before he left. Constable Wiebe also states that he had a general discussion with Dr. Newbery on communism and its possible attempts to penetrate local organizations.
I do not know how Dr. Newbery received the impression that he himself was under investigation, for such was certainly not the case. Dr. Newbery had been reported in the Sudbury press as having arranged for a press interview for the young men referred to and, as a responsible citizen and educator, he seemed the appropriate man to
Interim Supply
approach. Apparently constable Wiebe went to Dr. Newbery quite openly and in good faith and I would be reluctant to think that we have arrived at a time when the police, in the performance of their duty, may not approach the responsible citizens of any community for assistance.
You expressed some concern regarding the report which would be filed by constable Wiebe in connection with his visit. I can advise you that constable Wiebe's enquiry was of a routine nature and as no information of any particular value to the police was received, no report was filed. It was not until your letter was received that the Sudbury detachment of the Royal Canadian Mounted Police was asked for a report in order that a reply could be made to you. Naturally this report is now a matter of record.
As you have raised the question regarding inquiries by the Royal Canadian Mounted Police into the political views and activities of members of university faculties and student bodies, I would point out that the force has no interest in the political views of any Canadian, on or off the university campus. Subversion is another matter.
I hope this letter will clarify the matter in your mind and as I note you have sent copies of your correspondence to other persons and organizations, you may wish to consider directing copies of my reply to the same people.
I am not aware whether Maclean's magazine received a copy of the letter from Huntington college and I am not aware that its contents have been made public in any other way.
Reference was also made to the organization known as the voice of women. Here I have to state, as advised by the commissioner, that no statement has ever been made by the R.C.M.P. that this is a subversive organization.
Regarding the case of the 74-year old widow, now living in Regina, the R.C.M.P. are unable to identify any person with the details as they have been presented. I am aware that the leader of the N.D.P. has referred to this case in the house, but always without mentioning the name. If he will supply me with the name of the lady concerned and the information he has, in full confidence, I will undertake to have the matter fully investigated. According to the leader of the N.D.P. this case has extended over a period of 20 years, and yet I am informed by the commissioner that R.C.M.P. headquarters have been unable to find any file which could be identified with the lady in question. I might add that all members concerned have been questioned and even ex-members who might have had some knowledge of such a case, but without result.
Mr. Speaker, I should now like to deal with the complaints made by the hon. member for Nanaimo-Cowichan-The Islands, particularly that one in which he referred to a lady member of his constituency who was allegedly terrified as a result of being asked by a sergeant of the R.C.M.P. to spy on her neighbours. As the hon. member did not see fit to

Interim Supply
supply me with the name of this woman-I am not complaining about that because I do not think that there was any obligation on his part to do so-it was difficult to identify the file, and it was with some difficulty that a file has been located which seems to be related to the case to which he refers. The information, however, is completely at variance with the story told by the hon. member.
He has stated that without warning this lady was interviewed by an officer of the R.C.M.P. special investigation branch who called upon her after having ascertained by telephone that she was alone in the house. During the interview he suggested that she should undertake to spy on her neighbours and that her husband should undertake to do precisely the same job among his fellow workers at the logging camp in which he was employed.
The facts as they have been presented to me by the commissioner of the R.C.M.P. are the following. The complainant, whose husband is employed in the logging camp and normally away from home all week at his job, was not approached without warning by the R.C.M.P. The first knowledge the police had of this case was when this lady made a complaint to the local police detachment at Nanaimo, B.C. I should like to make it clear that the complaint was not made to the security and intelligence branch. She stated that she and her husband were being bothered by telephone calls and letters from a local man urging them to attend communist meetings and that he was pushing the propaganda quite heavily. She then requested information on how to deal with the person for, as she stated, she was fed up with him. This complaint was made in November 1962, and is a matter of police record in writing by the constable on duty when it was made.
It was as a result of this complaint that she was later interviewed by a sergeant in the security and intelligence branch. The statement that the sergeant had selected this couple for interview because of their name is incorrect, as will be seen from the facts. As to her being terrified, as stated by the hon. member, this accusation seems hardly to fit the fact that she had no reluctance in going voluntarily to the police in the first instance. This was not an approach by the police to this woman or her husband. It was the result of a complaint made by the lady herself to the police. The hon. member leaves the suggestion that for some sinister reason the sergeant wished to interview the woman in the absence of her husband. My information, which has been obtained from a report received prior to the hon. member's remarks in the house, is that the sergeant advised this lady to discuss the whole matter with her

husband. There is a great deal more that I could say about this case but I do not wish to do anything which would further identify, or embarrass, this lady any more than she has already been embarrassed in the house. If the hon. member is in any doubt about this being the case to which he refers, I will be pleased to discuss it with him further in private.
There is the other case which the hon. member has raised and which to my mind I consider very serious. When the hon. member raised it he made no mention of the name of the young man who had applied for entry into the Royal Canadian Navy, and of course I asked, as I did in the case of the other complaints, the commissioner of the R.C.M.P. to look into this case also. The commissioner replied that he was unable to locate a file which would coincide with the complaint which was put on Hansard, because, of course, he did not have the name. I listened on Sunday, as I am sure did many hon. members, to the report on the radio where the name was given and I was able to listen to the circumstances surrounding this case. I have since communicated with the commissioner and asked for a full statement. All I can say is this, that if the facts in this case are as stated by the hon. member in this house, then I have no hesitation in saying that there has been an injustice and that that injustice should be corrected, perhaps by the reinstatement of the young man. That I am unable to say, because I am not alone in that decision; it would be a matter which I would have to discuss with my colleague, the Minister of National Defence. But I can assure the hon. member that I personally intend, because I think it is a serious case, to look into it and see that justice is done.
I want to conclude-

I thank the committee, and I am almost at the end of my remarks. I want to conclude with two other matters. First, with reference to the R.C.M.P., I wish to say that my predecessors over a long period of time have paid tribute to this great body of officers, and I want to add my own tribute by saying that I do not think there is any police force in the world that can be compared with the Royal Canadian Mounted Police. If it was not an outstanding police force, certainly eight of the ten provinces would not be using it to do their policing. In

Quebec the premier of that province sought the services, as the house knows, of a former R.C.M.P. officer, to head the provincial force and many municipalities across this country have agreements with the R.C.M.P. to police their cities and towns. In Canada we have been fortunate indeed thus far in protecting the security of the state from espionage.
If there is any doubt on this point, may I refer hon. members to what is happening in the United Kingdom. There it has been found necessary to set up two royal commissions over approximately a one year period in an effort to ascertain by what means and under what circumstances employees of that government have been suborned to a point where they become traitors to their country. This speaks highly for the R.C.M.P. in our country. When regard is had to the fact that hundreds of thousands of inquiries are made each year then, indeed, I would go further than that and say it is surprising that mistakes are made in such few cases. Where there is legitimate criticism, the force has admitted its mistakes. But the vast majority of these cases have been in order, and I believe there has been no fault to find with the force.
Mr. Chairman, the next point is with reference to the parliamentary committee or inquiry, the point raised by the hon. leader of the N.D.P., I believe on the first day of the session. He referred to it again on Friday. I replied that having regard to the circumstances as I saw them then I did not think that at this time a parliamentary inquiry was warranted. I did not give any reason because it was difficult on orders of the day to go into that. However, I say now that the operations of a security service must to a very great extent be carried out secretly and without undue publicity. If the modus operandi of the secret service were made the subject of public discussion, there is no doubt that the service would cease to be effective. Sources of information would dry up and effective countermeasures would be taken by foreign agents to defeat the security methods employed.
I would like to point out to the house, and in particular to the hon. members in that corner, that I have been in the Department of Justice for barely over a month. Surely they will agree with me that in that time it is impossible to give the kind of study to this matter that it requires? So, under the circumstances I think I should be allowed to go into this subject and discuss it when there is more time, to discuss it fully in all its ramifications. I am not closing the door on the suggestion made by the hon. member, although I feel that at this time it is not warranted. However, there might be some other method by which
Interim Supply
some of these complaints could be done away with, and I am willing to study the matter carefully in that light.
In the meantime, if there are any further complaints then I would welcome representations to me by, or on behalf of, the persons concerned, and I can assure the house every such complaint will be thoroughly investigated.

Mr. Chairman, I must say that I am disappointed at the statement which has just been made by the Minister of Justice. I had expected more, from him and from this government, on this question than we have witnessed this afternoon. Over the years I have listened to a number of ministers of justice trying to defend some of the indefensible actions of the security and intelligence branch of the R.C.M.P., but I doubt if I have listened to a weaker defence than I heard this afternoon.
This is not a question about the fine police force that we have in the R.C.M.P. We all acknowledge that it is one of the finest police forces in the world. It is not the R.C.M.P. which is on trial this afternoon. It is the Minister of Justice, the Department of Justice and the administration of justice in this country. That is what is on trial, and the minister has missed the point entirely. No one here is complaining about investigations into subversion, the seeking out of persons who are guilty or may be guilty of treason. No one is complaining about the attempt to prevent espionage and to arrest those who are responsible for espionage.
The security of this or any other democracy requires that there must be a security force, but what we are objecting to is that under the umbrella of seeking to root out subversion we find interference with free speech and an attempt to intimidate people who are exercising their democratic rights. We submit that we will not strengthen democracy in our country by destroying democracy. The very essence of democracy is that there shall be free expression of opinion, that men and women shall be allowed to hold whatever views they may have, provided they do not go to the length of advocating the overthrow of the government by violence.
Many years ago Voltaire wrote an opponent of his who was being prosecuted by the state for his outspoken views, and said:
I disagree with what you say. but I will fight to the death for your right to say it.
This is the very essence of democracy.
The first of the two points which the minister missed is that the S and I branch of the R.C.M.P. have demonstrated they are

Interim Supply
completely incapable of differentiating between subversion and non-conformity. Let me give you some illustrations. On April 1, 1961, a nuclear disarmament parade and meeting were held in the city of Regina. I participated in the meeting which was chaired by a professor of the university. Other professors and local clergymen were on the platform, and students from Regina college were present. About a week or 10 days later-and this is only one instance, I think it happened on several occasions-a man in Yorkton was interviewed by a member of the R.C.M.P. who told him his son had taken part in this meeting and that if he did not stop associating with this kind of meetings he would get into trouble.
At a public meeting I made reference to this unfortunate incident. The then minister of justice came out with a public statement and said no such thing had happened, that the man had not been interviewed, and that there had been no attempt to intimidate him or his son. I did not bother carrying on a controversy through the press, but I asked the attorney general of the province of Saskatchewan to send the minister a verbatim copy of a conversation between the attorney general and this father which I have here. Then I asked the minister to read it, and see if he still contended that this man had not been interviewed and that there was no attempt at intimidation.
The then minister of justice wrote to the attorney general under date of July 6, 1961, and said:
I must agree that the facts as outlined by you concerning the approach to a citizen of Yorkton by a member of the Royal Canadian Mounted Police, are quite correct. I regret this very much, as the member of the Royal Canadian Mounted Police went beyond his responsibilities, although he undoubtedly acted in good faith in his attempt to advise the father of the individual concerned with respect to certain difficulties that might arise due to his son's connection with this movement.
The last paragraph of the letter says:
I want to repeat that I regret that the steps taken by the member of the Royal Canadian Mounted Police in this case, even though in good faith, went beyond his responsibilities, but I ask you to accept the fact that this was not in keeping with any desire on the part of this government, or of the Royal Canadian Mounted Police, and that there was not the slightest desire or intention to interfere with the political freedom of any citizen of Canada.
That is in a letter to the attorney general of Saskatchewan. It is not a public statement. It was sent by the then minister, Mr. Fulton, and so far as the public are concerned the minister's statement still stands, that there was no interference, no interview, and no attempt to intimidate this particular man.

I mention that example because I was personally associated with it. But many cases of a similar nature have come to my attention, in which the Royal Canadian Mounted Police have acted far beyond their responsibilities. I do not blame the whole R.C.M.P. I am simply saying that the S and I branch have demonstrated they are ill trained and inefficient to carry on this kind of work.
They should either be taken out of the R.C.M.P. or different types of individuals should be trained to carry on the work of providing security for our country. We are not going to strengthen democracy in Canada by allowing students to be intimidated through their parents, just because they happen to associate with other students and university professors in advocating nuclear disarmament or anything else they have a right to advocate which does not run contrary to the laws and constitution of the country.
The second point which the minister has missed entirely is that individuals who are investigated and branded as being bad security risks have no right of appeal. The minister said there is nothing wrong with asking a person a question. Of course there is not, but how does the accused person ask questions? There is no one of whom he can ask questions. Let me take again an instance with which I am perfectly familiar.
I became interested in this case as far back as January, 1950, when I was approached by a young man whom I had known as a child, and whose family I had known all my adult life. He was being discharged from the Royal Canadian Air Force on the grounds that he was a bad security risk, and this after seven years in the air force. I happened to be coming down to Ottawa to attend a federal-provincial conference, so I went to see the minister of defence at that time, a very good friend of mine, Brooke Claxton. He said there was nothing he knew about this case, it had simply been reported to his department by the police that the man in question was a bad security risk. The present minister says the R.C.M.P. do not make decisions, for instance the decision to dispense with a man's service. Of course, they do not. They just decide he is a bad security risk.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: No, they do not.

The Department of Defence had no information other than the report from the Department of Justice, which originated with the R.C.M.P. This alarmed me because I did not want to take on the task of defending a man who was a bad security risk; but the man came to me again and assured me he never had any contact with the communist party. I met his family. I

talked to his priest. I talked to the superior and teachers of the Catholic school which he had attended. I talked to officers with whom he had been associated in the air force. I could find no evidence that anyone had ever heard of this man being connected with the communist party so I asked Mr. Coldwell to raise this matter in the House of Commons. I have here photostatic copies of pages 3363, 3364 and 3365 of Hansard, for June 8, 1950, where Mr. Coldwell raised this case. When Mr. Coldwell asked Mr. Claxton about this man's communist connections the facts began to come out. The minister said: Well, he went to a Catholic college in Saskatchewan and he was put out for being a communist.
Then the light began to dawn. I recalled the incident myself when back in the 30's there had been an order at a certain Catholic college that no political parties were to be formed on the campus. Three young men formed a C.C.F. youth group, or C.C.Y.M., and they were expelled. When this young man was getting the regular security checkup the R.C.M.P. came to the college and found that he had been expelled for having helped to form a C.C.Y.M. group on the campus. As soon as I drew to the attention of the reverend father, who was in charge of the school and who had been there throughout the entire incident, the interpretation that had been placed on it he sat down and wrote a letter, a photostatic copy of which I have here, to the minister of justice of that time saying that this was a complete misunderstanding, that a great injustice had been done and pleading with the government to reinstate this man in the R.C.A.F.
No reply was received. I came down to Ottawa and I saw the then minister of justice and the commissioner of the mounted police. The commissioner of the mounted police informed me that the R.C.M.P. do not make mistakes-"this man was a bad security risk and he is still a bad security risk".
I wonder if the hon. gentleman would permit a question?
Surely.
Did he say that the C.C.F. movement at this school was the same as the Canadian communist youth movement?
Did I say so?
Yes. I just wondered about the initials that the hon. member used.

If the hon. gentleman cannot listen intelligently to what is being said I do not know what he is doing on the treasury benches. I said that this young man belonged to the C.C.F. youth movement or C.C.Y.M.,
Interim Supply
the co-operative commonwealth youth movement which had nothing to do with the communist party, never had and is never likely to have.
I am pleased to have that clarified.
What is more, the hon. member need not try to draw a red herring and use up my time because I am not going to be intimidated by that sort of silly question.
On a question of privilege, Mr. Chairman, there is no intention to intimidate. I merely wanted to get the facts straight so there would be no improper interpretation.

Will the hon. gentleman just sit down and keep his brain warm. When the present commissioner of the R.C.M.P. wrote a letter to Mr. Sidney Katz criticizing an article which appeared in Maclean's magazine, what did he say? Referring to this case he said that the man in question was an active member of the communist party. He said that during this period this man was an active member of the communist party. The man denied it, his family denied it, his church authorities denied it, the principal of the school he attended denied it, but the R.C.M.P. still say that he is an active member of the communist party.
Maybe the R.C.M.P. have information I have not got. I am quite prepared to admit that. What I am saying is that this man should have some right of appeal. Not only is he put out of the air force with a wife and family but when he gets a job his employer is informed inside of a month that this man is a bad security risk and he loses that job. That happened three times in a row. By this time he is left with an ulcer from worry and tension. When he gets out of the hospital he moves his family to another city and does door to door selling in order to make a living.
What I am saying is that we do not expect the R.C.M.P. can be infallible. No police force or security force can be infallible. What I am saying, and I have been saying it for years, is that in Canada we ought to do what they do in Great Britain where they have set up a judicial or quasi-judicial committee to which people can appeal, to which they can go with their counsel to be heard in order to clear their names.
I have on my desk here a score of cases of individuals who have applied for citizenship and have been told that they are bad security risks. I have cases of men who have gone to work for United States companies in this country and have been turned down, and it is hinted to them, "the report we get is that you are a bad security risk". There are cases here in the city of Ottawa of people

Interim Supply
who have been hired by the government and who find that they have been labelled as bad security risks. Maybe they are, but surely they should have the right to be heard. Surely it is the essence of democracy that they have the right to face their accusers and know by whom they are accused and with what they are charged. Neither the R.C.M.P. nor anybody else has a right to be prosecutor, judge and jury, the right to say that this man or this woman is a bad security risk and that closes the whole matter.
I have a case here of a man who came from Great Britain to live in the city of Regina. He went to apply for citizenship and was interviewed by a Corporal Young of the R.C.M.P. He was told: We know that you attend communist meetings, we know that you have communists come to your home and you visit their homes, and we know that you receive communist publications. When he begins to ask who these subversive people are it turns out that he is chairman of the local New Democratic party club, that he visits back and forth with people in that club and that he receives literature from the Canadian peace research institute. The crowning indignity was the suggestion made to him that it would be a lot easier for him to get his citizenship papers if he would agree to stay in the organization and report on the other people with whom he was associated.
Again I am quite prepared to concede that this man may have associations of which I do not know. But he should have a right to go before some impartial body, to be represented by counsel and to be told why he is not being given his citizenship papers, because he has not yet been given them. The minister simply says: Give me the names and I will look into the matter. What does he do when he gets names? He gets a report from the R.C.M.P. and, as Commissioner Wood said to me, "The R.C.M.P. do not make mistakes".
So we are dealing with the omniscient and omnipotent. What is the use of giving anybody names? The minister mentioned the case of the widow in Regina. I noticed that the R.C.M.P. commissioner in his letter to Mr. Katz described this story as a fabrication, just simply untrue. I am prepared to substantiate that story. This woman, described as a widow in Regina, is only a widow recently. She was not a widow during the entire period. I have known her and her late husband for the past 30 years. This woman is a Christian pacifist who periodically-I do not say every year but periodically, probably every two years-was visited by an R.C.M.P. officer and questioned as to her views, what books she reads and so on. This is because

she was listed during the war as a Christian pacifist. She has never made any secret of her Christian pacifism.
I do not happen to share the views of the pacifists, but I admire their courage and I certainly defend their right to be pacifists. When this woman talked to me about this, I offered again and again to take this matter up with the Minister of Justice. She said, "I do not want any trouble; I would just as soon put up with these calls and forget about
them.	" I only became really indignant on the last call of which I have any record when the officer said, "Your wife is a very good friend of the wife of the minister of agriculture for the province of Saskatchewan. Can you tell us whether or not he is a communist? I will come back tomorrow to see if you can give me some information." I said, "When he comes back, send him up to my office; I know the minister of agriculture much better than you do and I will give him all the information he wants." Needless to say, he did not appear.
The minister says, you give me this woman's name, and I will look into it. Is the R.C.M.P. so inefficient, are there so many people in Regina being investigated, that they cannot find this one case? Are they trying to tell me they have not been interviewing this woman? I will make a deal with the minister. I will not give him the name so this woman can be badgered, but if the minister will undertake to show me the file, then I will give him the name. Then, I can see the file and not just accept the word of the inscrutable, the imperturbable R.C.M.P.;
then,	I will be able to see this file and I will be prepared to discuss this case with the minister.
This woman is not complaining. She is over 70 years of age. They cannot bother her very much in the few years she has left. I simply use this case as an illustration of the way in which a peace-loving, orderly, law-abiding citizen has been badgered and bothered by the security and intelligence branch, or whatever branch it is of the Royal Canadian Mounted Police, simply because she holds views that are not in conformity with those of the mass of the people in the community.
I should like, therefore, to suggest three things. I want to suggest, first of all, that I think the time has come to take the security and intelligence branch out of the Royal Canadian Mounted Police; to staff it with highly trained people who are skilled in looking into subversion, who know the difference between non-conformity and espionage, who know the difference between people who are ready to commit overt acts

of treason and people who merely have a point of view that is different from the point of view held by most of those in the vicinity.
The second suggestion I make is that the government give consideration to setting up in the government a tribunal or quasi-judicial committee to which individuals may come with their counsel and say, "I have been denied a job", or "I have been kicked out of the armed forces; or I have been refused citizenship on the grounds that I am a bad security risk. I have a right to see the evidence against me. I have a right to face my accusers. I have a right to be heard before my name is slurred and the names of my children are slurred; that is all I am asking." Surely, this is a reasonable request in a democracy.
The third suggestion I make is one which I proposed in a question on orders of the day. I think that there ought to be a select committee of this house look into the whole procedure for dealing with subversion and maintaining the security of this nation. It would probably have to meet behind closed doors part of the time. I admit there are difficulties in administering a security system. I admit that in the kind of world in which we live today, security is important. However, I contend that, equally important with maintaining security is the maintenance of those basic democratic institutions upon which this country is built. It will be of little value to destroy totalitarianism across the seas if in the process we incur totalitarianism here. I suggest, Mr. Chairman, that in the long run liberty is indivisible. If I allow my neighbour's civil liberties to be encroached upon today, my liberties will be in danger tomorrow.

Agreed.

I am simply contending that we, as members of this high parliament, and all of us who treasure democratic institutions, ought to be properly concerned about what appears to be a violation of the uses and purposes to which a security force has been put. I agree with the minister when he says he has only been in office a little over a month. I do not hold the minister entirely responsible, except that I do hold him responsible if he does not proceed to do something about this matter. The situation has been getting worse. There have been more and more violations. The representations that
Interim Supply
have been made by the Canadian university teachers association are something to which attention should have been paid long ago. The minister now has a responsibility; the ball is at his feet. I have enough faith in him and his associates to believe that they will not allow this sore to fester much longer, that they will take some steps to correct the situation. I can assure them that if they do not, then we in this group will continue to raise this matter again and again and again, because I can assure you that I will not allow some of these cases that have occurred to be repeated without making protests that will be heard from one end of the country to the other.
Since it is just about five o'clock, and I do not want to take up too much time of the committee, I wonder if I could call it five o'clock so I will be able to keep some continuity in my remarks?

If that were done, we would be very glad to make the time available from nine to ten for private members' hour, in order to obtain continuity.
Dealing with the question raised by the minister, may I say that I doubt if the extra hour would get us through. I believe the hon. member for Comox-Alberni wants to raise a fairly pressing matter.

However, I am in the hands of the committee.

If the hon. member has a question which he wishes to raise, I have no objection to proceeding. However, I do not feel it should be understood that we conclude by nine o'clock if all the matters that need to be raised have not been considered.

speakeroldname: Mr. Heber E. Smith (Simcoe North) moved:
subsubtopic: AMENDMENTS CONCERNING PHYSICAL AND MENTAL CONDITIONS
speechtext:
That, in the opinion of this house, the government should give consideration to the advisability of enlarging the definition of a disabled person in the Disabled Persons Act, and the regulations pursuant thereto, to take into consideration such factors as the physical condition, the mental condition and the age of the applicant, and other factors which create a condition of permanent unemployability.
He said: Mr. Deputy Speaker, speaking for the first time in the twenty sixth parliament I should first like to congratulate you on your appointment as chairman of committees. I should also like through you to congratulate the Speaker on his appointment, and the deputy chairman of committees. I wish you well in your tenure of office.
My father taught me to believe that man's first public duty was to help those who were least able to help themselves. Nothing that 1 have learned since has changed my mind about that early teaching. Indeed, I now know it to be a basic tenet of Conservative philosophy. I think that government responsibility is no different; it too should be directed first to helping those who are least able to help themselves. Sometimes in the vision and glamour of all-embracing welfare schemes this rule and lesson is forgotten. The people I am going to talk about are not those who will benefit from a contributory pension scheme, because they do not earn enough; they are not the people who would benefit from the New Democratic party's "airy fairy" promises of full employment, even if such promises could be fulfilled, because they are unemployable.
Who are these people? I think that every hon. member who is interested in his constituents knows dozens of them; he talks to them almost every day he is in his riding. I am quite sure there are many thousands of them all across Canada. Mostly you will find them in the age group of 45 to 65. They are all permanently unemployable, usually through a combination of circumstances. Their age contributes to it; their physical condition in some form contributes to it; their lack of training and their lack of education, their inability to absorb further training or further education, contributes to it. Some of them, because of mental and psychological conditions, are unable to work in the complicated industrial society that we find today; they just will not fit into an assembly line. All of them are left behind.
Where are they now? You will find many of them on permanent relief rolls. Some of them you will find being kept in genteel and not so genteel poverty by their families. Some are drifting from job to job from day to day, doing little else than distorting our unemployment statistics. Hon. members might say, why not keep them on welfare? In my opinion welfare was never designed to meet a permanent condition. Welfare, as I understand it, is designed to tide people over temporary difficulties and temporary embarrassments. I do not think these people should have the humiliation of being permanent welfare wards, because the conditions which cause their unemployability are largely completely beyond the means of correction by themselves.
There are many things that could be done and many acts that could be changed. I have thought to bring forward this motion relating to the Disabled Persons Act because these people are disabled. I would like to read the present definition:
For the purpose of the act and these regulations, a person shall be deemed to be totally and permanently disabled when suffering from a major physiological, anatomical or psychological impairment verified by objective medical findings which is likely to continue indefinitely without substantial improvement and, as a result thereof, such a person is severely limited in activities pertaining to normal living.
I think that perhaps the main objection to the definition is the "normal living" part because, as now interpreted, "normal living" is considered to mean the ability to perform activities such as hygiene, feeding, dressing, walking, stair climbing, use of hands, speech, vision, hearing, writing, and reading. Unemployment is not a factor in reaching a decision. I think it is time we had a new definition that is broader and takes into consideration more of the activities of normal living. Particularly I refer to that of employment. Can they be gainfully employed? Is there anywhere they can be usefully and gainfully employed? For that reason I suggest that the four important factors which ought to be considered under this new definition would be, the physical condition of the person, the mental condition, the age and the permanent unemployability which flows from the first three conditions.
It will be pointed out, no doubt, that the provinces have to be consulted, that this is co-operative legislation I realize that. However, I do not think we will have any difficulty in getting co-operation from the provinces, because it was a Conservative government in Ontario in 1954, under the premiership of Leslie Frost, that took the lead in putting this legislation forward. In
[The Chairman.]

1963 another Conservative government in Ontario has taken a step which answers the problem of a great many of the people who would come within the categories I have mentioned. I refer to the recent changes by the Hon. Louis Cecile in the assistance to widows and unmarried women's regulation under the general welfare assistance act, which now provide that widows and unmarried women over the age of 60 who have no means are eligible for a pension. This covers a reasonable proportion of the people with whom I have come in contact.
There is another small point in relation to this regulation that I would like to touch upon generally, although it is not covered within the terms of my motion. I refer to those cases of married couples where one person, either the husband or the wife, is disabled and qualifies under the physical requirements of the act but is disqualified by the very low ceiling income that is permitted for people like that. One example that has come to my attention recently in the city in which I live is the case of a man who is permanently disabled. His drugs bill is $55 a month. He and his wife have two boys in the family. The wife is endeavouring to keep the home together, and she earns $45 a week. By reason of his earnings, the husband is disqualified for the D.P.A. pension and yet she is expected to do the impossible of keeping the home going and buying his drugs on $45 a week. In cases where one or the other spouse is disabled the ceiling should be lifted substantially so that the $65, or whatever the amount of the pension may be from time to time, could be used for the necessary home care of the disabled spouse.
Another case which came to my attention was that of a small farmer who lives in my own riding. He has ten or eleven children. His wife is incurably ill with a disease such as multiple sclerosis. He is not a man who makes a large income. He has to keep his oldest daughter at home to do the housework. Yet by reason of his modest earnings his wife's pension is only $14 a month. This means that although the eldest daughter has to stay home and work he has no means of paying her even a modest wage for her services. Although such circumstances as these are not covered by the terms of my motion, I should like earnestly to commend this thought to the government in the hope that some changes might be made in this regard also.

The resolution before the house on the motion of the hon. member for Simcoe North (Mr. Smith) seeks to enlarge the definition of a disabled
