person in the Disabled Persons Act and the regulations pursuant thereto. I should like to compliment the hon. member upon the birth in his noggin of this very Liberal notion. I only wonder why he did not do something about it during the last six years while he was sitting on this side of the house.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENTS CONCERNING PHYSICAL AND MENTAL CONDITIONS
speechtext: We did.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENTS CONCERNING PHYSICAL AND MENTAL CONDITIONS
speechtext:
It was a Liberal government which introduced the Disabled Persons Act. It was assented to on June 26,	1954,
and proclaimed in force as of January 1, 1955. It was, and is, another jewel in the long string of social welfare measures initiated for the benefit of our people by the Liberal party. It currently provides that 50 per cent of $65 monthly, or 50 per cent of the allowance paid by the province, whichever is the lesser, shall be contributed for each eligible recipient over 18 years old. Federal payments to the provinces are made monthly in arrears and not in advance. Thus, there is a sharing of cost between the federal and provincial governments under this joint scheme, but each province administers it for its own territory.
During the fiscal year ended March 31, 1961, there were 16,453 applications considered by the provinces. Of this number 6,398 were approved, 9,331 were declined and 724 were not completed. Federal contributions to the provinces and territories amounted to $16,385,819.54 in that year.
The hon. member, by his resolution, seeks to broaden the act under discussion so as to admit more of the 9,331 who were declined but it must be borne in mind that many of these were entitled to receive, and did receive, benefits under other joint federal-provincial schemes, particularly the Unemployment Assistance Act. This latter act came into effect only six months after the Disabled Persons Act and was intended, no doubt, to complement it. It has done so with good, but not complete, success, and as long as there is any loophole to be plugged, I for one along with the hon. member for Simcoe North, am all for plugging it.
I am not certain, however, that broadening the definition of the evaluation of invalidity is the answer. It may be more desirable to increase the benefits to those clearly entitled under the present definition, than to set a precedent by advancing the borderline to increase the number entitled.
All hon. members will bear in mind that presently the whole scheme of pensions for all categories is being reviewed in pursuance of declared Liberal policy, and the contents of the speech from the throne.

Disabled Persons Act
We know that there will shortly be introduced into this house and this country a comprehensive contributory portable pension plan. Contrary to what the hon. member has said, the government is studying not only survivor benefits but disability benefits. If agreement can be obtained with all the provinces there would seem to be no reason why this new comprehensive plan should not include disability benefits. Then all our social security insurance would be written into one new national policy which would be fair to all across the land, and the act under discussion would be repealed.
However, whether the act stands or is repealed, there is need for concern in this matter and I can assure the hon. member for Simcoe North that his motion with regard to extending the benefits on the basis of unemployability is being thoroughly studied by actuarial, social and medical experts in the Department of National Health and Welfare.
Mr. Speaker, there are many disability benefit programs in existence in different countries. There is, however, no uniformity of disability evaluation under such programs. In Canada the rule or definition for disability evaluation is contained in one subsection of the disabled persons regulations under the Disabled Persons Act (Office Consolidation, 1961). Section 2, subsection (2) thereof provides:
"For the purpose of the act and these regulations, a person shall be deemed to be totally and permanently disabled when suffering from a major physiological, anatomical or psychological impairment verified by objective medical findings which is likely to continue indefinitely without substantial improvement and, as a result thereof, such person is severely limited in activities pertaining to normal living."
With respect to administration, assessment of permanent and total disability under the Disabled Persons Act is carried out by joint federal-provincial medical review boards in each province, which are guided by the disability evaluation manual (first revision) September, 1957, prepared by the Department of National Health and Welfare. Chapter 11, interpretation of definitions, provides the official interpretation of the specific phrases in the definition. On pages 5, 6 and 7 an explanation is given of the key phrase, "as a result thereof, such person is severely limited in activities pertaining to normal living". The criteria to be followed in making an assessment of functional impairment in terms of activities of normal living are set forth. It is clear that the determination of disability is based upon loss of functional capacities imposed by the impairment. On page 8, the responsibility of the medical review boards

in referring all potential rehabilitation cases to a rehabilitation assessment team for appraisal and for beneficial therapy is stressed.
In addition to medical appraisal, a social report designed to provide medical review boards with a clear picture of the applicant in his normal circumstances is required. It provides evidence of the degree of actual handicap which the impairment imposes, and should also indicate the extent to which the applicant has overcome difficulties in the past. It helps to identify those persons who would be capable of helping themselves if they received special assistance.
Great Britain, New Zealand and Australia have various disability benefit schemes in effect. In each country there is some provision for benefit for loss of working capacity as a result of permanent disability.
The international social security association in its report on the activities of the working group on the problem of harmonizing the criteria for the evaluation of invalidity, published in its bulletin for October, November and December, 1962, recognizes several elements posed by the complex problem of invalidity evaluation. Interested hon. members will find in this report in the library that the working group, as a first step towards the harmonization of criteria for the evaluation of disability, has recommended certain principles and methods. The original intent of the Disabled Persons Act was to meet the needs of a group of severely disabled persons who, for mental or physical reasons, were unable to provide care for themselves and who presented problems not merely of unemployability but in respect to capacity for self-care. A sickness survey, undertaken some years before the act was passed, indicated that this group was a sizeable one and deserved the next priority in the progressive development of social security measures that was being undertaken by the Liberal government of the day.
It was specifically intended that the concept of employability would not enter as a basic consideration in this program. There were two or three important reasons for this. One was the extreme difficulty of defining employability. In everyone's experience there are persons who are able to surmount the most severe handicaps and achieve a livelihood through the maximum utilization of their remaining capabilities. A further factor was the determination of the government at the time to keep the concept of rehabilitation to the fore, and not to make allowances available to persons who should be encouraged to utilize to the full the rehabilitation services that were then available and which were being encouraged through the federal-provincial rehabilitation program. This was a

point that was emphasized by many of the best authorities in the field. To emphasize this point, the act itself provided that even those who were eligible under the permanent and total disability clause could be further assessed for rehabilitation or approved therapeutic measures. This provision was included to ensure a positive and constructive approach by encouraging rehabilitation and therapy whenever benefit was considered likely to be derived.
The Disabled Persons Act from the very outset provided a valuable measure for those eligible within its terms. All provinces took advantage of it, and for many years there was a steady increase in its coverage. It continues to the present time to perform a necessary and highly valuable role in Canada's social security program as indicated by the case load which in March, 1963 reached 50,600.
Even at the time that the Disabled Persons Act was being developed, discussions were proceeding between the federal government and the provinces for the development of a program which would help to meet the needs of those who could not qualify under the terms of the Disabled Persons Act. I am referring again to the Unemployment Assistance Act which, after discussions with the provinces in 1955, was enacted in 1956 retroactive to July 1955. Under this measure the federal government pays approximately one half the costs of assistance to residual groups of persons not aided under such special programs as those for the aged, the blind and the measure under particular consideration now, the Disabled Persons Act.
Mr. Speaker, there is not sufficient public knowledge of the role this legislation has played in the development of provincial programs of general assistance for the residual group in need, and also for special groups such as the type of person that is envisaged in this resolution. The way in which the provinces have developed their general assistance programs under this legislation has, of course, varied from province to province-indeed, this has been held to be one of the advantages of the legislation in that it has allowed the provinces to undertake measures which are suited to their particular needs. Many provinces assist all types of needy persons under roughly similar provisions, but in a majority of provinces some special attention has been given to some or all of the types of persons referred to in the resolution. It may be of interest to hon. members to have some specific examples of the measures that exist for the group referred to.
In Newfoundland, social assistance may be granted to persons who are temporarily or permanently unable to work because of
Disabled Persons Act
mental or physical incapacity. The program is administered by the province in a manner similar to disabled persons allowances, and the benefits under the program may be adjusted to take into account any dependants of a disabled breadwinner.
The province of Nova Scotia also provides, under part I of its social assistance act, for assistance to disabled persons between the ages of 18 and 65 who are not able to qualify for disabled persons allowances. It is my understanding that this benefit does not vary with family size, although there are other provisions in the act to provide for disabled fathers with dependant children; in the latter case, the provision of assistance is, of course, primarily related to the importance of providing support for the children.
In addition to the general provisions that it has for any persons who are unemployed and in need, the province of Quebec has a special program for persons who have been unemployed for more than 12 months, most of whom would be in the category under consideration. The benefits under this program are, as in the case of Newfoundland, related to the number of persons in the family, and the program is administered by the Quebec social allowances commission. It is also relevant to note that the province has developed a special program for widows and single women from 60 to 64 years of age, and undoubtedly in many cases assistance under this program because of need could be related to some form of disability.
There are two programs in Ontario for which federal sharing is now available and which are of interest in this discussion. Provision is made for assistance to families with dependant children in which the need is related to the unemployability of the father, including commitment to a mental or other institution. This program is administered by the department of public welfare through its regional offices throughout the province, and the benefits are paid on the basis of what is referred to as a needs test, under which the level of aid is related to the requirements of the family, as well as any other income that it might have. With effect from May 1, the province of Ontario has also developed a pension program for widows and single women from 60 to 64 years of age as mentioned by the hon. member for Simcoe North (Mr. Smith). This pension is paid on the basis of a means test and carries a maximum benefit of $65 per month, the same as that for disabled persons allowances.
Because of the similarity of their programs, I might refer to the provinces of Alberta and Manitoba together. These provinces have enacted legislation which provides for the payment of a social allowance to any person

Disabled Persons Act
who is unable to earn an income sufficient to pay for the basic necessities of himself and his dependants because of age or physical or mental ill health or incapacity that is likely to last for more than 90 days. Hon. members will note that this is the type of comprehensive coverage referred to in this resolution. The costs of these allowances are, as in the case of the programs referred to above, shared under the Unemployment Assistance Act and, Mr. Speaker, you may be interested to note that in March 1963 there were about 17,000 persons, including dependants, assisted under the social allowances program in Alberta. I believe that the program is now fully in effect in that province, but it is my understanding that the province of Manitoba has adopted a more gradual approach in the implementation of its program, preferring to proceed with it at a pace which will be in line with its fiscal and administrative capabilities.
There are two provinces to which I have not yet referred, British Columbia and Saskatchewan. In British Columbia social allowances are payable to any persons who are unemployed and in need, without making a distinction between employability and unemployability. The program is administered co-operatively by the province and its municipalities, and the benefits are related to the number of dependants in the recipient's family.
In Saskatchewan, assistance to the group referred to in the resolution would, I believe, be provided under two programs. In cases where there are dependant children in the family and the need could be related to the disability of the father, provision is made for assistance through the aid to dependant families program. Other persons in this group can be assisted through the municipal social aid program, and in both cases the amount of assistance paid is related to the requirements of the recipient and his family. It is my understanding that there is in Saskatchewan a good deal of provincial-municipal consultation concerning the provision of social aid, and that every effort is made to assure that the needs of recipients are adequately met.
Hon. members will note from this review that the framework within which assistance is provided varies from province to province, and that the coverage of existing programs is broader in some areas than in others. This, of course, is to be expected when the fiscal capabilities of the various parts of the country are borne in mind, and I should hasten to emphasize that the federal government stands ready under the Unemployment Assistance Act to share in any more broadly

based programs that the provinces may see fit to adopt for the disabled or other needy groups.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I too want to congratulate the hon. member for Simcoe North (Mr. Smith) for bringing in this resolution and bringing to the attention of the house the difficulties I am sure most hon. members have had with respect to the definition of total and permanent disability. At the same time I want to say that I have listened with interest to the remarks of the hon. member for Spadina (Mr. Ryan). It is really too bad he is not a member of the cabinet because we have got far more out of him about what the government is doing and intends to do in the field of social welfare than we have been able to get out of ministers sitting on the treasury benches. But, even if we have to get it from a backbencher, it is good to know that an overhaul of our social security legislation is coming and that all these various matters will be dealt with.
This is the first time I have realized that the proposed contributory portable pension scheme would include something for disabled persons at 18 years of age, because after all that is what the Disabled Persons Act provides-for assistance where it is needed to people at that age.
Mr. Speaker, we have been asked by the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Miss LaMarsh) to contain ourselves. It will be easier to do this, now that we have this backbench assurance that we are going to get some pretty extensive social security legislation during this session. The hon. member for Spadina (Mr. Ryan) made some references to the origins of the Disabled Persons Act. Some of us who were here when it was introduced can remember the circumstances quite well. There had been repeated representations across the years for legislation in this field, but like other such representations they had not been heeded until about 1953 when the prime minister of that day, Mr. St. Laurent, received a personal letter from a disabled individual, a letter couched in such terms that it made a personal appeal to him. The word we got was that he felt so concerned about the plight of incurables and disabled persons that he decided something ought to be done. As a result of that, the research done in the department came into play and we got the legislation.
Well, it was good to get it, and it is good to know that the number of people cited by the hon. member for Spadina are being assisted under that legislation. We agree with
Disabled Persons Act
him that we have to have a broad welfare policy. We have to look to the needs of our people under various categories and various headings, and we should not just try to solve the problem in the simplest way.
Our welfare policy has grown up like Topsy, and it is time we had a good look at it. The very review which the hon. member for Spadina has given, showing the differences that obtain across the country, makes it obvious we need a wholesale review of our social welfare policy. But it still stands as incontrovertible that if we are going to have -and I am glad we have-legislation providing allowances for disabled persons on the basis of disability, then the definition of that disability should be such as to provide allowances to persons who are readily recognized as disabled.
I am sure that my experience is not unique. I have had a good many instances where individuals, who to me were obviously disabled, have not been able to get the allowance because they could not meet the terms of the definition. The fact is they were still alive. They could move about a bit. I am going to read a few sentences from a letter about one case, and I am sure that other members can produce similar letters. I quote this in support of our contention that the definition as it stands under the Disabled Persons Act is far too narrow. The letter I have in my hand I will identify as one written to me by the chairman of the old age assistance and blind persons allowances board of Manitoba. That same board handles allowances under the Disabled Persons Act. The chairman wrote me about a case I had been taking up with him, and he said in part:
It seems quite apparent that his-
The reference, of course, is to the individual about whom I had written.
-heart condition is such that he is unable to work, but this condition would not prevent him from going about the regular routine involved in normal living if he does not try to do things too hurriedly.
That is not my description. I saw the man and I had written to the chairman of the board in Manitoba that just as a layman seeing the man I could see that he was disabled and unable to work. This is the chairman of the board admitting to me that because of the man's heart condition he is unable to work, but saying that this should not prevent him from going about the regular routine involved in normal living provided he does not do things too hurriedly. So he could not get the allowance.
The chairman went on to tell me in this letter that up until a certain date this individual had had a job. He had been running a dishwasher machine in a certain hospital

Disabled Persons Act
in Winnipeg but he had had to give up that job because of an operation he had to have on his stomach. The man already had difficulty with his legs, he already had a heart condition such that he could not work, and on top of that he had an operation on his stomach. I quote now from the letter:
After his operation he was too weak and short of breath to go back to this job. I was concerned about this case-
This is the chairman of the board writing to me.
-and discussed the details somewhat fully with members of the medical panel. I suggested to them that the loss of most of the stomach in the recent operation-
This is on top of the heart condition and so on.
[DOT]-might well make the applicant eligible. Their response to this was that while it might make him feel a sense of discomfort and weakness after eating it was not in effect disabling.
Here is a man over 60 years of age with a heart condition such that he cannot work, a stomach operation as a result of which most of his stomach is removed and he feels a sense of discomfort and weakness after eating, but still he does not qualify as a disabled person within the meaning of the act. This particular individual was at the time of this correspondence between the ages of 60 and 65. It was ascertained that his wife would shortly be 65 so the suggestion was made, of course, that at that time the wife could apply for and no doubt obtain old age assistance in the province of Manitoba, and that once she got old age assistance it would then be possible for her to apply for social assistance-

speechtext:
Yes-on the basis that her husband would be her dependant. Surely the hon. member for Spadina will agree with me that, though it is fine to say there are these various programs it does not exactly qualify as a definition of human dignity to say to a man in this position that the only way in which he can qualify for any kind of assistance at all is by waiting until his wife is 65 so she can get old age assistance, and on the basis of that get extra so-called relief for him.
This is one case. I admit it is the most glaring of the recent ones I have had occasion to deal with. I know we have all had cases like this one. But I submit that even if there is going to be the overhaul of social welfare legislation that the hon. member for Spadina has promised on behalf of the Liberal government it is still incumbent upon us to take another look at the definition of total and permanent disability in the Disabled Persons Act. Along with the hon. member for

Simcoe North (Mr. Smith), the hon. member for Cariboo (Mr. Leboe) and others I think that the definition should be liberalized so that the act will really provide allowances to persons who in ordinary terms are disabled.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I was glad to hear the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) give a former prime minister, Mr. St. Laurent, credit for introducing the Disabled Persons Act. I recall that the bill was introduced in the house by the present Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Martin) when he was minister of national health and welfare. Prior to that time the Canadian welfare council in 1954, I believe, submitted a brief to the government, probably in anticipation of such legislation, and they attempted to classify unemployed persons under three heads. Under the first one they included the group who were obviously permanently and totally disabled and had no prospects of any improvement or cure. These people in future, they thought, would obviously receive payments under the act.
The second group comprised those persons who had some handicap but were able to do some work and thus support themselves in whole or in part. The third group consisted of those people who fall between the extremes of the other two groups and about whom we are concerned here. They are those people who cannot be classed as totally and permanently disabled but are unable to work and make a living. In presenting his resolution today I suppose the hon. member for Simcoe North (Mr. Smith) is proposing to include some or all of this particular class of people under the act.
Last year the act was before the house for amendment and the purpose of the amendments was twofold. One purpose was to increase the maximum monthly allowance to $65 and the other was to increase the over-all earnings that a person might have. In the case of a single person the increase was $180 and in the case of a married person it was $360. I remember that at that time members of the house urged the minister to go a little further and enlarge the definition. He read the definition to us and I think that the definition, which has already been read by two members today, would cover the particular cases that the hon. member for Simcoe North has in mind. It would include those with a physical or mental disability or impairment.
So far as age is concerned, persons cannot qualify for a pension under this act at the present time unless they are 18 years of age. I could not conceive of any province wanting to share with the dominion and making of

payments to anyone 70 years of age and over because the federal government bears the full cost of old age security in this area.
I have been somewhat concerned over the years with the difficulty we have had in getting some of these people included under the act. I know that medical men are not aware of the different cases that might be included. We fill out a form for the applicant, and it is a rather extensive form. We send it in to a review board. The review board may send back for more information or may refer the case to a specialist. If there is any difference of opinion between the applicant's medical man and the review board, then the case is sent to an appeal board which is made up of a doctor appointed by the federal government and one appointed by the provincial government. If these two doctors do not agree, then another provincial medical man is appointed.
Since this is a cost-sharing program, the payments are made after a means test. The provincial government sends out an investigator to look into the financial situation of the applicant. I do know that these investigators inquire into other things as well. I recall that last year one hon. member stated that a particular patient, and he was a patient because he had been sick before making application, had incurable heart disease. He was declared to be permanently and totally disabled; yet because this particular investigator found he had walked out into the garden, his application was disallowed. I do not think this sort of thing should be permitted.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I wonder if I could ask the hon. gentleman a question? What would he think of having the doctor certify this person as being totally disabled and then if the board is not willing to accept that certification another independent doctor might be asked for his opinion. I know the hon. gentleman has had a good deal of experience in this field over the years. My feeling is that the local family doctor knows the case better than any government official who is miles away and never sees the person concerned. If the board does not want to accept the decision of the family doctor, then let them call in an independent physician in the area to give his opinion. I believe this has been done over the years under the mental health act in the province of Ontario. I should like to get my hon. friend's views based on his experience over the years.

Mr. Speaker, I did not intend to participate in this debate but I should like to congratulate the hon. member for Simcoe North (Mr. Smith) for having introduced this motion to call the attention of the house on the urgency of amending the regulations governing assistance to the disabled.
In my riding as elsewhere, it often happens that people are deprived of the assistance to which they would be entitled because, after all, one does not have to be totally incapacitated to be entitled to the assistance given to the disabled. In fact, this legislation which was put on our statute books by a Liberal government, as the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) stated so rightly a moment ago, could be amended with the co-operation of the provincial governments so as to cover certain cases of invalids who are absolutely unable to get any work.
In the past, I have met constituents of mine who could get around by themselves in their own house but who could not do any kind of work. I am thinking especially of epileptics who could not work at all, not even in an hospital, for instance, if they wanted to do so. That is why I wonder if it is truly in the spirit of the law to require that such a person should try to find some work.
It seems to me that there should be some way of changing the law in that respect and, once more, I commend the member for Simcoe North for having called the attention of the house on that situation.

It being six o'clock, the hour for private members' business has expired and the house will resume the business which was interrupted at five o'clock.

The house in committee of supply, Mr. Batten in the chair.

Mr. Chairman, this is the first opportunity I have had to speak as a member of the opposition. It goes without saying that I am not happy to find our party sitting in this part of the house, but it does seem to me that there are certain compensations to being in the opposition. Being of Irish ancestry I have been much taken with that old saying, "Oh, I don't care who the government is; I'm agin 'em". Knowing the members of the treasury benches as I do, I feel there will be many opportunities when I will be called upon to criticize. If I am going to damn the government, I feel there will be times when I will be doing so most forcibly and I want to assure my hon. friends over there that in those circumstances I shall be doing so most happily.
[The Acting Speaker (Mr. Batten).]
Tonight, however, I intend to be quite gentle. I want to speak on a subject that is, I think, rather important, not just to my immediate area but because it reflects air policy and its importance throughout Canada in the approach that the air transport board and the government itself may take toward new air services. We have just had inaugurated from Edmonton to Calgary by Pacific Western Air Lines what they call an air bus service to Calgary. About three years ago the runways of the new international airport at Nisku started to be used. T.C.A. then changed their operation from the municipal airport at Edmonton to the Nisku airport and the only air service we have had connecting Calgary and Edmonton has been by T.C.A. via Nisku.
I pointed out in a speech in this house in 1960, and again in the 1960-61 session, that this means an extra half hour taxi ride out to Nisku, that if T.C.A. were not prepared to operate out of the municipal airport at Edmonton, someone else should be allowed to do so. I feel that connecting flights could reasonably operate from Calgary to Nisku, but for just intercity flights without connections across Canada the convenience of Edmonton and Calgary businessmen could only be met with a service that operated out of that airport to ours in the middle of the city. It has been three years now since the runways were opened at Nisku, and the main building will soon be completed. I believe there is a total investment in Nisku, when finished, of approximately $25 million. There is naturally much pressure on D.O.T., considering the size of that investment, to see that the facilities at Nisku are used to the fullest extent possible. There is also much pressure on the Department of Transport by various groups and people in the city of Edmonton who feel, for one reason or another, that our airport, located as it is in the heart of the city, is too dangerous to operate.
Because of this latter approach the Department of Transport not too long ago raised the safety standards at the Edmonton municipal airport to the extent that it was no longer permissible or possible for any air line to give service out of that airport by Viscount aircraft and, as I said, they changed to Nisku. I thought that this raise in the safety regulations was unnecessary, that there was already a sufficient safety factor and this further, more stringent regulation was not needed from a safety viewpoint and had the effect of depriving us of the benefits of good service. There has been a suggestion now that the Department of Transport is considering raising these safety regulations. I

would suggest that the only reason they would be doing this is to try and discourage commercial air service out of our downtown airport. I would suggest to the committee that the commercial service out of Edmonton consists in good part of the Edmonton-Calgary service and in part of the service to Grande Prairie, Peace River, etc., all of which, because of the very shortness of the flight time, can be added to immeasurably if they are served out of the municipal airport. The flight time from Nisku to Calgary is only 45 minutes. To get on a T.C.A. aircraft you are supposed to arrive 20 minutes early, with a 30 minutes taxi trip to get out there. That is 50 minutes before flight time. Then there is further time at the other end waiting for your bags, so it comes to about two hours in all for the trip.
It may be said that T.C.A. lose a considerable number of their passengers to not only the private automobile but also the C.P.R. Dayliner which gives very good service running from the centre of town to the centre of town. I am sure the Department of Transport in their ideas of further improving safety regulations at the municipal airport are going to have the blessings, if not the connivance, of T.C.A., which I can understand. They feel the air bus service of P.W.A. is going to take away most of their business. I merely suggest to the Minister of Transport that really P.W.A., with their air bus service, will be able to operate and make a profit out of just that business that T.C.A. would never have gotten anyway, because it was too inconvenient operating out of Nisku. With the air bus service there are no reservations. A man merely goes out to the airport a few minutes before plane time; he gets on board with his bag in his hand, is sold a ticket on the way down, and when he gets off there is no waiting for his baggage. He saves at least an hour. The only way T.C.A. could compete with this sort of competition would be to inaugurate such a service.
I would like the Minister of Transport to take a look, if he would be good enough, at my speeches in this house on this problem. They are to be found, for 1960 at page 4469 of Hansard, and for the 1960-61 session at page 5112 of Hansard, where I asked T.C.A. for this sort of service, where I pointed out to the Minister of Transport these problems, and where I pointed out that the first result of this new, expensive airport at Nisku was a poor air service for Edmonton. I can assure the minister that, while I am always ready, willing and able to give the government a good deal of abuse when I think they need it, and
Interim Supply
I can foresee considerable criticism descending on the government's head, because there is such a large investment at Nisku which has not been used as much as the planners had hoped at the time it was started, if he will resist the efforts of those who would like to divert everything to Nisku to make it look better, he will never hear a complaint out of me that the costs are too high at Nisku. We in the city of Edmonton appreciate very much the fact that jets, with their noise problem, are not operating right out of the city, that we do not have in Edmonton the sort of complaints that cause so much trouble at Dorval. We also appreciate the extra safety factor of these very high speed aircraft being out in the country where the maximum safety regulations can be observed. But there is such a thing as being too safe and too cautious. Air regulations are already so much more stringent and our traffic is now so much more safe that to increase it further would have the effect of entering the realm of unreality. I suggest to the minister before the government makes the safety regulations even more stringent than they are it should envisage precisely what this would mean to air traffic compared with the situation which exists for railway, motor vehicle, truck and bus traffic in our cities. I suggest that if these other forms of transport had to operate up to the safety standards which now prevail in connection with Edmonton municipal airport it would be impossible for 90 per cent of the traffic now on our streets and railways to run at all. Heavy truck traffic would not be allowed to enter our cities, and all level crossings would have to be abolished if trains were to continue to run.
I am aware that air crashes are spectacular and that they are given a great deal of publicity. But I am also aware of the fearful toll on our highways and the rather large number of train-car collisions. Obviously, in this age of fast travel people have become accustomed to taking a certain amount of risk and will accept a certain amount of risk in keeping with the realities of modern transport necessities. I am suggesting that a fair comparison of the handicaps under which our air transport now has to operate in the name of safety as compared with those imposed on other fields of transport would show that flying has already been hobbled with ten times the strictness known to any comparable type of transport. I am suggesting that for three years the businessmen of Edmonton and Calgary have had to put up with an air service much decreased in usefulness. They had lost much of the value they might have been getting out of it long before we began spending these huge sums of money at Nisku. The arguments in favour of the development

at Niksu will not be strengthened by imposing regulations which make it impossible for aircraft to operate out of the municipal airport.

The site is a most convenient one and the city of Edmonton is very lucky to have it now. I suggest the minister reflect a little on the type of aircraft which is now being developed. I suggest he use a little imagination to envisage the direction aircraft design is taking. He might give consideration to the fact that short run aircraft and vertical take-off aircraft are now being developed and that within a few years the so-called dangerous aspects of travel to and from municipal airports may have been removed as a result of changes in the type of aircraft in operation. I cannot see how this or any other government could justify taking steps which might have the effect of closing down this airport before we have really had a chance to enjoy the benefits of it.
One reason why I was anxious to make this speech tonight is that I want no suggestion that the government is sticking its neck out with regard to the safety factor. I think the safety factor is more than sufficiently high. I want to emphasize the importance of this airport to communications with the north. This balance of convenience affects the people of Grande Prairie and Peace River as well as those of Edmonton and Calgary. I am sure the people who live in northern Alberta are anxious to save that amount of time which makes it possible for a businessman to get a day's work done on a trip into town. I hope the minister will do me the honour of reading my previous speeches on this subject; that he will look at the reasons for possible criticism and make a realistic appraisal of these air regulations. I say the city of Edmonton now has the highest standard of air safety in the country and that any suggestion of changing it to a still higher standard is merely a way of depriving us of the air service for which we have waited for so

long. Next, I say that Trans-Canada Air Lines must have a hand in any such suggestion and that T.C.A. really cannot say Pacific Western Air Lines is running any competition to them because, as I have pointed out, P.W.A. is flying customers that T.C.A. would not have a chance to get, anyway.

This airport was planned, but construction had not been started when the Conservative government came to office in 1957. However, if these regulations are changed again, resulting in the loss of the air service we now have, he will wish he had never been born.

Mr. Chairman, I am always rather inclined to feel sorry for the Minister of Finance whenever a debate develops on an interim supply motion. He usually finds himself in the position of sitting listening to matters concerning the sins of commission and omission of all his colleagues. However, I suppose under the principle of cabinet responsibility that is just one of the crosses he has to bear.
I am glad to see the Secretary of State sitting close to him tonight because I think that his most laudable desire to get this motion disposed of fairly quickly could be hastened if he would assure us that we could have a proper statement on the government's intention and policy with regard to a matter I want to raise. I might add I would like to see both the Minister of Fisheries and the Secretary of State for External Affairs present tonight to give a full statement on government policy with regard to the whole matter of the north Pacific fisheries. I do not see them in their places at the moment, but perhaps the Secretary of State could ensure that we do have, if not from one of those ministers at least from someone else, a proper statement of government policy on this matter.
There are many matters of importance which I could rise to deal with at this time, but I have selected this particular matter because I feel it is in the nature of an emergency subject, and also because of the fact that I am rather disturbed and distressed by the somewhat cavalier manner in which this whole question appears to have been swept under the rug by the new administration.
Hon. members who were here during the last parliament will recall that the whole subject matter of the international north Pacific fisheries commission and some recommendations it made to the Canadian government were a subject of interest and concern during the proceedings of that parliament, and that quite a number of questions were

addressed to the minister of fisheries as to what the intention of the then government were in this connection. While the former minister was perhaps a bit evasive in some of the answers he gave, nevertheless I think it is fair to say the house could get from his answers the distinct impression that, before any decision was made with respect to Canada's position on the recommendations made by the commission, there would be an opportunity for a full review of this matter before the standing committee on marine and fisheries.
Of course, as we all know, parliament was dissolved before anything of that sort took place. However, I am sure it would not have escaped the attention of some of these who now sit on the treasury benches that the then prime minister, during the period when parliament was dissolved, intimated in a statement he made on the Pacific coast that a decision on this matter of great importance to us in British Columbia would not be made until parliament had been reconvened and there was an opportunity for a full study of the whole question.
However, as the house is aware, or perhaps I should say as the house is not aware, the present government has made a decision in respect to this matter. I say that perhaps the house is not aware, because to my knowledge the only mention of this whole question and the action of the government upon it has been made outside the house. The new Minister of Fisheries has not even had the courtesy to stand up under motions, after parliament met, and make an announcement of what the decision of the government has been, although in reply to questions which were addressed to him later he has indicated the government has made a decision on this matter.
Mr. Chairman, I was a member of the house when we had a former Liberal minister of fisheries, and I think it is fair to say that discussion of fishery matters during that particular period was very largely non-partisan in its nature. If I might offer my own explanation as to why that was largely the case, I feel it was because for the most part hon. members of the house, who at that time had a particular interest and concern in fishery matters, while we might not always have been in complete agreement with the minister, nevertheless felt we had an adequate and full opportunity of looking into all fishery matters as they arose from time to time, and of participating in the discussions leading up to policy that was developed. I raise this aspect of the question because I feel it would be a sad thing indeed if this new parliament should get off com-28902-5-39J

pletely on the wrong foot so far as discussion of fishery matters is concerned.
I want to report to the house that during the time since I first became a member of it-and as hon. members realize I have not been a member continuously since 1953- during the period of those 10 years I have been trying to devote some of my attention to matters relating to the fisheries on the Pacific coast, and I have never known the fishermen of British Columbia to be so deeply disturbed and concerned as they are now about the matters involved in this international north Pacific fisheries commission. Every fishermen's organization in British Columbia has taken a position opposed to the action which the government apparently took on May 8. The united fishermen and allied workers union, the Pacific trollers association, the native brotherhood, the native Indian fishermen's organization and the fishing vessel owners association are all opposed. I am fully aware of the fact that spokesmen for the fish companies have agreed with the action taken by the government. However, when there is such a wide gulf in opinion on such a basic matter I suggest that the Minister of Fisheries and the government were certainly ill advised indeed to come to the decision they did on May 8, particularly when parliament was so shortly to convene and when it would have been possible, I am sure, to have the full co-operation of all parties in the house in setting up immediately the marine and fisheries committee to look into this whole question.
This question may appear to some members of the house to be a matter of relatively minor concern, and in order to put it into perspective I should like to express its importance in these terms. If words were to come to this chamber that the whole of the three prairie provinces of Canada were in imminent danger of becoming a vast desert, I am sure that would be considered by members of the house to be a matter of urgent significance no matter from what part of Canada members might come. I suggest to the house that the north Pacific basin occupies an area considerably larger than the three prairie provinces and that its resources, which we share, of course, with some of the adjacent nations, in the long run may very well be more important and significant, more rich and varied and more capable of helping to sustain a high standard of living among the peoples of the world than the total resources of the three prairie provinces. Therefore I suggest that this is a most serious and important matter and the decisions that may be taken at this time may set a course which will affect not only the people of this generation but generations of Canadians yet to come.

The history of the matter is that 10 years ago the Canadian government entered into a convention with the United States of America and Japan for a treaty which would conserve and develop, according to its stated intention, the fishery resources of the north Pacific. That treaty set out some basic principles of agreement. It also set out some temporary arrangements which would apply during a certain period until our fishery scientists had had an opportunity of surveying the then still largely unknown resources of this vast fishery.
This treaty is subject to notice by any one of the contracting parties that a year from the date on which notice is given it will expire. I understand that the earliest date that such a notice can be given by any one of the parties is June 12 of this year. In reply to a question I asked the other day of the Secretary of State for External Affairs he indicated that preliminary negotiations are starting almost immediately in Washington in respect of this treaty. He did not indicate whether any one of the contracting parties had given any indication that it intended to serve notice of the termination of the treaty or, indeed, had served any notice whether or not it desired any formal renegotiation of the terms of the treaty. What he did indicate in his reply to me was that there was to be some preliminary discussion of a continuation of the abstention principle in the treaty.
This matter came to the fore last fall, of course, because of the recommendation of the international north Pacific fisheries commission when they recommended to the contracting parties to the treaty that there should be a watering down of the original abstention principle provided in the annex to the treaty. I am fully aware of the fact that the way the treaty is drafted and the way the annex is set out it is quite within the technical prerogative of the government to alter the basis of the abstentions, to which Japan agreed, without formal ratification by parliament. But I suggest to the committee that it is contrary to the whole spirit and approach with regard to what I have felt is the proper way to deal with fisheries matters in this house for the government to have taken action in the way it did.
I find it difficult to understand that the present Minister of Fisheries, even though he comes from one of the eastern maritime provinces, should have been so unaware of the significance of this matter and of the interest and concern which have been displayed in British Columbia, particularly in view of the questions which some of his fellow Liberal members were asking during the last session of the last parliament. Certainly implicit in those questions was a desire on the

part of the Liberal members from British Columbia that this matter should go before the marine and fisheries committee at an early date. On November 23, 1962 the hon. member for Vancouver South put this supplementary question to the then minister of fisheries:
Would the minister assure the house that before the government accedes to this recommendation we shall have an opportunity to debate the possibly tragic consequences?
I probably do not need to remind those on the treasury benches that the hon. member for Vancouver South is now Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources, and it is rather surprising to me that he did not take the trouble to inform his colleague, the new Minister of Fisheries from New Brunswick, that it would be very advisable to convene the marine and fisheries committee in this connection.
I tried to point out a parallel of just how tragic these consequences could be. I am not saying that at the moment we are in imminent danger of exhausting the fishery resources of the north Pacific, but I do know enough of the history of my part of the world to know that the original development of white settlement on the west coast of Vancouver island was based upon the sea otter trade. The sea otter is something I have never seen and no British Columbians see any more because it is extinct. Then there was the fur seal trade. They became almost extinct until conservation measures were taken. A little later there was the problem with respect to whales. It was found necessary to bring about some sort of international arrangement for the conservation of whaling in the north Pacific. So it has been with our salmon and our halibut.
Tragic consequences can overtake us rather quickly, as has been proven more than once by actual events in the history of the west coast exploitation of the resources of the Pacific.
I am not going to refer to all the questions that were asked, but I should like to draw attention to the fact that the hon. member for Coast-Capilano, who I understand is fairly close now to the ear of the Prime Minister- at least for the time being when he is not talking about selling out crown corporations -asked the then minister of fisheries as to whether or not this matter was going to receive the attention of the marine and fisheries committee. As late as January 30, he was asking the minister if we could have this matter before the marine and fisheries committee.
I should like to contrast that with the answer I was given the other day, on May

29, when I addressed a question to the Minister of Fisheries. He said this, as reported on page 416 of Hansard:
-I wish to state that when the government decides to convene the standing committee on marine and fisheries, the house will be advised accordingly.
Now, if I have ever received the ministerial brush-off during my time in this house, that was it. I am sorry that the minister is not here tonight. I do hope that some of his colleagues will give him a good jacking up about the manner in which he is apparently approaching this whole subject.
I do not know that I need to say a great deal more. Certainly, I cannot attempt, nor do I think it is necessary, to launch into a discussion of the ramifications of this treaty, what should go in and what should not in so far as a renewed or altered treaty is concerned. I believe I have made it clear that I consider that sort of thing to be properly the subject matter of a hearing in the marine and fisheries committee when we could have some of our competent scientists before us to answer questions and when we could have adequate representations from the fishermen and others concerned with the fishing industry.
I do hope that before this debate concludes we are going to have some sort of indication of the attitude the government is going to take in connection with this most important matter.

It is more than just the commercial fishermen who are concerned. I would quote just two sentences from a brief, Mr. Chairman, and after I have quoted this excerpt I will give the committee the name of the organizations who are supporting this resolution:
The recommendation of the international north Pacific fisheries commission to open northern B.C. and northern Alaska waters to Japanese fishing fleets poses a serious threat to the future of B.C.'s fishing industry .. . The commission's action was a form of appeasement and allows Japan to get her foot in the door which could lead to future net fishing of our salmon off the west coast of Vancouver island by Japanese fishing fleets accompanied by mother ships equipped with refrigeration or canning equipment. It is of the utmost importance that our government must do everything in its power to stop this future threat and protect our heritage.
This is a resolution submitted by the amalgamated conservation society. The following organizations are members of this society and are co-signers of this brief: Victoria Saanich inlet anglers association, south Vancouver island rangers, Esquimalt salmon club, Oak bay anglers, the Chinook club, royal Canadian naval anglers association, the Cowichan bay salmon club, Victoria fish and game protective association, the Victoria chamber of commerce, the Saanich inlet boatmen's association, the Pacific trollers association, the Victoria outboard club.
The point I want to make is that there is much concern on the whole of the Pacific coast, not only as to the government's action in accepting the recommendation of the commission, but the eyes of the west coast people, through these organizations that I have quoted, will be on Washington when the renegotiation of this treaty takes place. I hope the Secretary of State will keep in mind what he indicated tonight, as I understood him, that there will be no firm commitment by the government until such time as there has been an opportunity by this house to discuss the renegotiation of that treaty.

Mr. Chairman, this is one of the first opportunities for me to bring to the attention of the government some of the problems that are arising from a scheme in the province of Ontario in which the federal government obviously intends to participate. On June 1 of this year the Ontario government proclaimed the first portable pension program in Canada. Both the Conservative government and the present government have stated that portable pensions for Canadians must first be brought into a national pension

scheme to replace our old age security program, and at the same time such a scheme must take into consideration the rights of provincial governments in this field.
I think more leadership should come from the federal government, rather than waiting for one of the provincial governments to do something in this particular field. What would have happened if the federal government had waited, when they decided to implement unemployment insurance, until all the provinces had a scheme of their own that the federal government could bring under their wing as a national insurance program? The same is true of family allowances. If we had waited until family allowances were implemented by the provinces, and then the scheme had been endorsed by the federal government, we might have had a very different scheme, on a patchwork basis, than we have at the present time. I believe this matter of pensions is just as important as any social legislation to which the Canadian people have given their attention. During the recent election campaign, particularly in northern Ontario, I think all the candidates of all political parties were of the opinion-

Mr. Chairman, I wonder whether the hon. gentleman would permit me to interrupt-I am not seeking to do so in anything but a conciliatory spirit-to raise a question as to whether, since this portable pension program scheme and the old age security program are a part of the program envisaged in this session of parliament and are not yet in operation, this is the appropriate time at which this subject should be raised.
This is a time when hon. members have a right to raise grievances with respect to matters that are now being carried out by the government. There was an opportunity in the debate on the speech from the throne, there will be another opportunity during the budget debate, there will be a still further opportunity on various supply motions, and there will be an opportunity when the legislation itself is brought before parliament. I am really appealing to the hon. member who is seeking to raise a formal point of order. Does he not feel at this time, when the government is seeking supply in order to carry on the ordinary administration, and seeking to get it so that we can get on with the rest of our program, that he would not be willing to defer this discussion until one or the other occasions I mentioned, without a formal point of order being raised?

If this is a formal point of order I do not think it need detain us long. I do not intend to go into the ramifications of pension programs in general, but this is a

matter which has been discussed in the speech from the throne and we are now being asked to vote about one third of the total estimates for this year. speechtext: My reply to that is very brief. If hon. members opposite would give us supply it would enable us to get on with our program and bring the pension legislation down that much earlier.

speechtext: Nothing is stopping you from putting it on the order paper.

On this point of order, the subject with which I am dealing is not so far divorced from the responsibility of this government as has been suggested. A major consideration with regard to any pension plan, whether it be in Ontario or any other province, is the income tax exemptions which are allowed in respect of this plan. This places responsibility on the shoulders of the federal government. In 1945, the previous government brought in, through the minister of finance of that day, Mr. McCann, a direction covering pension plans for the purpose of the Income Tax Act established by the taxation division of the Department of National Revenue. I suggest the reason this was disallowed was because vesting rights in this pension plan could not be negotiated between some of the major companies in this country, companies which already have had plans in operation with the federal government. In 1959, it may be remembered, the Conservative government again brought in a regulation affecting the vesting rights of pension plans. But the government of that day again withdrew the direction, which was issued by order in council, for the same reason namely that they were having great difficulty with the vesting rights in the income tax division.
You may be surprised to know, Mr. Chairman, that in connection with that new plan in Ontario an observation has been made by the Montreal Trust Company pension division in the following terms:
It would appear that employers are seeking to avoid the legislated provisions and control of the act covering benefits in sharing or deferred profit sharing plans as a vehicle for providing supplementary benefits which do not come under the control of the act. However, income tax concessions, particularly from the employee's standpoint-
I should like to point out that the Ontario pension plan has not met one of our basic needs in northern Ontario where there are movements of labour interprovineially on a considerable scale. Many people live in Ontario and work in Quebec. This is common in the Noranda area. Then there are large numbers of people living in northern Quebec who travel into Ontario to work in the mines. Thus, any plan which depends on the provinces for its implementation, must find itself seriously limited, since, as I say, people travel from one province into another to work and, when they retire, probably move into the second province to live. Thus, there is a need for a national attitude toward pension plans. Many of the miners in northern Ontario have recently been asked to leave their homes and places of employment in

order to live in northern Manitoba. So the problem is not just one between Quebec and Ontario; it is national in scope. Some of the men I know might have been working at Belle island. Then they would move to Sea island. The next job might be in Alaska or even in the United States. The federal government has agreed to participate in this Ontario provincial scheme, but since the inception of that scheme many shortcomings have become apparent to the workers concerned.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: I should bring to the attention of the hon. member that he may not discuss the merits of this provincial statute dealing with portable pensions. Although I do not wish to restrict discussion in any way I submit to him that he should not confine his remarks to a matter which relates exclusively to an Ontario statute. I believe this is what he has been doing for the last minute or so.

With due deference, Mr. Chairman, that was not what I was doing. The vesting rights have already been discussed on a number of occasions. My point, which I will not labour, is that I believe the federal government have a responsibility in the matter. I could quote from the literature which was circulated in my area and the ridings of other hon. members of the Liberal party indicating that this was one of the first considerations which the government would take under discussion. There is a limit on the act passed in Ontario, and the federal government still has time to provide legislation to implement a better plan than that envisioned by the provinces. The government can certainly count on our assistance, but they should not wait until the provinces are ready with pension plans of their own so that the federal government can provide the umbrella under which they can operate. I suggest this matter should be properly planned. The present government has probably had considerable time to discuss the commission's report at great length, which contains all the necessary information to provide Canada with a very far reaching pension plan serving the needs of the people, instead of doing it on a patch-work basis and allowing the provinces to put this sort of legislation into effect.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, when I intervened in the debate this afternoon, I referred to a complaint made by the hon. member for Nanaimo-Cowichan-The Islands. I told him at that time that I was not able to deal with the case because I had not obtained the report from the mounted police. I have now obtained that report and I should like to make a statement with reference to it.
The question raised by the hon. member for Nanaimo-Cowichan-The Islands on Friday 28902-5-40
Interim Supply
last concerned the dismissal from the royal Canadian navy of Gordon Harry Knott. Although the name of this man was not supplied, inquiries made by the R.C.M.P. during the past week end at the west coast have revealed that, in this case, a serious error has occurred.
The R.C.M.P., as far back as 1958, had been informed by a very responsible person in that community in which the Knott families had lived that Gordon Harry Knott's father, Wallace Knott, was a brother of one Ernest Leon Knott. The source of this information was in a position where he might be expected to know of such a relationship. Until this week end, this same source of information was still of the same belief. After Gordon Harry Knott had joined the royal Canadian navy in October 1961, the R.C.M.P. was requested to make the usual security check. At this time, and in another community, a further reliable source of information was questioned as to his knowledge of the Wallace Knott family. This person held a responsible position in the community and stated that he knew Wallace Knott very well and was also acquainted with his brother, Ernest Leon Knott. This was confirmation of the information already held on file by the R.C.M.P. Here we had, in this matter, two reputable sources of information, living in different communities, each claiming a good knowledge of the Knott families, stating that Wallace and Ernest Leon Knott were brothers. It was on this basis that the R.C.M.P. felt themselves on firm ground in making their report to the navy.
Following the hon. member's statement to the house on Friday and the location of what appeared to be the appropriate file, although the name had not been advanced, a most intensive investigation was launched at the west coast during the week end. Eventually a source of information, of undoubted reliability, was located which made it quite clear Ernest Leon Knott and Wallace Knott were not brothers.
Under the circumstances, Mr. Chairman, I can only tender a very deep apology to this young man and his family, not only for the inconvenience but for the embarrassment which has been caused. I am taking this matter up with my colleague the Minister of National Defence to see how he, Gordon Knott, if he so wishes, can continue with his interrupted career.

Mr. Chairman, I should like to express my very great appreciation for the minister's frank statement, which I am quite sure will be accepted wholeheartedly by this boy's family. Thank you very much.

Interim Supply

Mr. Chairman, I am sure all of us are grateful to the minister for taking this very speedy action, but if ever there was proof of the need for setting up some appeal body, it has been shown here tonight. Here is a man who was dismissed from Her Majesty's forces on the strength of statements from two people who allegedly knew the family but who it turns out did not know the family. To have a man condemned on the basis of tittle-tattle, on the basis of rumour, on the basis of information given by unintelligent people is surely not good enough. A report has been turned in on flimsy evidence, the kind of evidence on which I submit, Mr. Chairman, you would not hang a dog.
As I said this afternoon we are not condemning the R.C.M.P. as a force. What we are saying is that the kind of people who have been handling security and intelligence are in a great many instances lacking the right kind of qualifications; that these people are ill-trained and ill-informed and in many cases completely unfit for the task they are carrying on. Surely it ought not to lie with members of the House of Commons to have to raise individual cases like this. If this young man's case had not been raised by the hon. member for Nanaimo-Cowichan-The Islands, he would probably be still like the young man from the air force in Regina- peddling goods from door to door with a bar sinister across his record. Members of parliament have more to do than deal with individual cases like this, and the Minister of Justice has more to do than to be badgered by them. Surely the time has come to set up a proper tribunal or quasi-judicial committee to where people like this can go; where they can take their counsel, call their witnesses and be heard; where they can know what is the evidence against them. If they have nothing to fear and come honestly and disclose all the facts, then undoubtedly they will be given a clean bill of health. If they cannot, then of course the security branch has done a good job in that it has discovered some person who is a menace to the security of this nation. I urge the minister that in light of this illustration which he himself has given tonight the government should take into very serious consideration the setting up of some board of appeal to deal with these cases so that members of parliament do not have to deal with them on the floor of the house. I for one am prepared to leave it to the minister and his good sense to deal with this. If it is not dealt with when the estimates of his department come before the house, I must say we shall want some further information regarding what the government proposes to do in dealing with cases of this nature.

Mr. Chairman, there is one matter which I should like to speak about for a few moments. I should like to know, and I think this committee would like to know, what has been the decision of the government as to a review of a policy initiated by the previous government and whether they are going to follow it through with the expenditure of certain money in the next two months, which expenditure we are now discussing. I am referring to the finalizing of plans which could result in a multi-million dollar expenditure. I am talking about that part of the interim supply now before us asking for a sufficiency of money to complete the plans of, and to call for tenders for, the construction of a multi-million dollar drug addiction treatment centre on the west coast of British Columbia.
This matter of drug addiction is a serious one, particularly in the province of British Columbia. It is going to cost a great deal of money to cure the addicts, to see they do not return to drug addiction, and to get rid of narcotic pushers. Therefore, it is of the utmost importance that we feel sure in the finalizing of plans, towards which money will be allotted during the next two months, that our policy on the treatment of drug addiction is going to prove beneficial, particularly when the taxpayers will be called upon to spend many millions of dollars.
Mr. Chairman, I am raising this matter now because I am of two minds as to whether or not the policy outlined by the previous government and which has resulted in the initiation of the present plan, is the correct one. It is the policy of placing the drug addicts, by compulsion, in an institution for treatment and later releasing them. However, throughout the world, and particularly in the United States, it has been proven that a similar plan does not cure drug addicts.
Has the government, since it took office, gone into this question? Has it made any study of its policy regarding the curing of drug addicts and the controlling of the narcotics racket? Has it accepted and is it prepared now to state that the correct policy is that which was initiated by the previous government?
I raise this matter because over the years we have been treating drug addicts as criminals and putting them in penitentiaries. There they are cured of their drug addiction because they cannot get drugs, but when their sentence is over and they go back into society, unfortunately in the majority of cases the majority of these men and women who have not had drugs for years go right back and become addicts again, of their own volition or because of the pressure put on them by narcotic pushers. Surely, sir, that

amply demonstrates that institutionalizing on its own is not the answer to this most severe and serious problem?
Surely we should recognize by now that addicts should be treated as sick persons, should have curative treatment and under doctor's orders should receive, on a diminishing basis, their drug requirements? But, no matter what is done, it should be on a basis that when they were released to society they are not subject to the drug pushers, and the only way to get away from that is to take the profit out of the drug racket.
The spending of millions of dollars on an institution may still leave that cancerous sore because of the fact that drug pushers can still make a profit and can still persuade people into the habit of drug addiction. I do not want to delay the house any longer but this is a vital problem, and as we are being asked now to vote moneys for June and July for the completion of the plans-and I have read in the press that tenders are being called-I feel it my duty to raise the matter on interim supply and to question whether the government has given consideration to this entire question.
If the government has considered what is the best policy to be pursued in Canada to remove this curse of drug addiction, is it the government's contention that it is going to go along with the solution of the problem through treatment in an institution which is going to cost millions of dollars in the province of British Columbia? If it feels it should go ahead on this particular line then I feel that at some future time there should be a further discussion in this house of the problem in all its aspects.

Mr. Chairman, before clause 1 carries may I say the Minister of Finance seemed a little unhappy that after his general invitation to members to put questions to him most of the questions were directed to other ministers. I do not like to see the

Ways and Means
Minister of Finance unhappy, especially just 10 days before he is going to bring down his budget, so I am happy to accommodate him by asking him some questions about matters that do come under his jurisdiction.
As the minister will recall, he has been asked a number of times already this session by members in various quarters of the house about certain civil service matters. The minister has a very disarming way of answering these questions. He tells us these matters are under active consideration and we get the impression something is going to be done, but I have the uneasy feeling that these answers are copied almost word for word from the answers given by the previous minister of finance. He was disarming and genial as well.
You flatter me.

speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader; Whip of the N.D.P.
speechtext:
The minister was pretty outspoken before he moved over to the treasury benches about the speed with which things could be done. He had a lot of ideas. Does he think it is fair to the civil service that so many categories have had to wait so long for the pay increases that became effective for most categories on December 10 of last year? Can this not be dealt with very soon?
I will save the minister the trouble of bobbing up and down by asking all my questions now. There is also the problem of civil servants who retired after the retroactive date of the pay increases but before the pay increases were announced. In other words, these civil servants were working during the period in which there were pay increases but because of the date of their retirement they did not get them. The minister has said this is being looked into. How long does the looking into process have to take?
Then there is the question of collective bargaining for civil servants, and this has been indicated as something to which the government is committed. I take it this comes under the responsibility of the Minister of Finance. How much longer are we going to have to wait for this?
Another question I have raised on a number of occasions is the improving of pensions of civil servants already retired. I remind the minister that for many years we in this house urged that something should be done to improve the pensions of those who were being asked to live on very small amounts. It was argued for many years that this could not be done, that these pensions were matters of contract, that the regulations were set and there was nothing that could be done about the whole matter. I have to give a bouquet to the last government. They made a breakthrough in this field and did bring down the first legislation that actually increased the

pensions of civil servants who were already retired. But though the previous government made a breakthrough I do not think they did enough in terms of the amounts that were provided or in terms of the people who were covered. Retired civil servants are still pressing for action in this field.
There are other problems with regard to temporary employees and the various orders in council and treasury board directives that have affected these people. Frankly, Mr. Chairman, we do not think that the minister should take too long in coming forward not just with an assurance that these matters will be considered but with a definite statement that something is being done.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: May I say to the hon. member, who is an old trade unionist and will understand these operations, that when I answered questions before and said these matters would be dealt with promptly I did not mean that they would be dealt with overnight. On the preamble-

speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader; Whip of the N.D.P.
speechtext:
Before the preamble carries, may I ask the minister a question about one of the provisions in this bill? I do so because earlier this evening he said that after there had been a complete review of the 1962-63 expenditures an accounting would be placed before parliament and parliament would be asked to give formal authorization. I realize that is about all we can expect a new government to do with respect to a previous government's expenditures.
What I wanted to ask was this. Is that something that is still to come, or has that been tucked into clause 6 of this bill?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
That is something that is still to come, Mr. Chairman.
IMr. Gordon.1

speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader; Whip of the N.D.P.
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, can the minister tell us what clause 6 is about?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Yes, Mr. Chairman, I shall be glad to. Clause 6 is new and is required because of a strict interpretation of subsection 4 of section 28 of the Financial Administration Act which was first enacted after the period of general financing by special Governor General's warrants in 1958.
It was intended to ensure that special warrants would be open to discussion in parliament on the first occasion on which requests were made to parliament for further supply. It was obviously not drafted in contemplation of a recurrence of the unusual situation of 1958, but I am advised that under present circumstances its strict interpretation would require the inclusion of the amounts authorized by special warrants, in the old year 1962-63 to be included in the bill. Rather than intermingle and confuse the financial records of the two years, and because it is the government's intention to provide parliament with a complete accounting in respect of 1962-63 later in this session, this bill includes only those special governor general's warrants which provided for expenditures during April and May, 1963, the first two months of the current fiscal year.
The special warrants which supported government operations during the final months of the year 1962-63 will be described in detail in a report on supply for 1962-63 which will be tabled later this session and which will be followed by a special appropriation act dealing solely, but completely, with the expenditures and accounts of that year. In this respect, the proposed practice is modelled exactly on that followed in 1958.

Preamble agreed to.
Title agreed to.
Bill reported.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wonder
whether the house leader would announce the business for tomorrow and, profiting from today's experience, not interrupt proceedings at five o'clock and things of that nature.

speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should begin by apologizing to the hon. gentleman's susceptibilities for my interrupting. It was not very successful and perhaps it would not be very wise to repeat it.

Tomorrow we will continue with the debate on the motion of the Prime Minister to set up the committee on matters relating to defence. As soon as that is completed we will take the resolution preceding the bill to set up the economic council. If that should be completed-

That is enough.
Business of the House Mr. Pickersgill: I think it is perhaps just as well to indicate as far as possible what else would be taken up. If that is completed we would hope to take up the resolution preceding the bill to set up the department of industry.
It being eight minutes after ten o'clock the house adjourned, without question put, pursuant to standing order.
